# J.M. Struijk

> Independent author of practical, non-clinical books and articles for adults with ADHD, autism, and AuDHD. Late-diagnosed with both, and writes from lived experience. Published through JMS Media Group LLC (Wyoming, US). 11 books in print across three series and one standalone guide, available on Amazon, plus 18 long-form articles and a glossary of 32 terms on jmstruijk.com.

Each book and article targets one specific way ADHD or autism shows up in adult life, rather than offering general productivity advice. Every book stands alone; readers can start anywhere.

## Articles

Long-form writing on ADHD and autism, from lived experience. Not clinical guidance.

- [The ADHD tax: what it actually costs, and why budgeting advice keeps missing it](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-tax-what-it-costs/): The ADHD tax is money lost to late fees, forgotten subscriptions and replacing things you own. Where it goes, and why budgeting advice misses it. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Why ADHD brains overspend, and what actually helps](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/why-adhd-brains-overspend/): Impulsive spending with ADHD is rarely about wanting things. How reward, time and emotion drive it, and the fixes that actually work. Published 2026-10-21.
- [ADHD and debt: why payoff plans keep failing, and what to do instead](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-debt-and-payoff-plans/): Debt payoff plans assume consistency, which ADHD does not reliably supply. Why the usual methods fail, and how to build one that survives a bad month. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Hyperfocus without the crash: using the good days without paying for them twice](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-hyperfocus-without-burnout/): Hyperfocus gets called an ADHD superpower, usually right before it costs you a week. How it works, and how to use it without the crash. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Diagnosed with ADHD as an adult: what the first year is actually like](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-diagnosis-as-an-adult-first-year/): Relief, grief, and rereading your own life. What the first year after a late ADHD diagnosis tends to be like, and what helps. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Finding out you are autistic in adulthood](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-in-adulthood-late-diagnosis/): What changes when you find out in your thirties or forties that you are autistic, why so many adults are missed, and what the first months involve. Published 2026-10-21.
- [AuDHD: what it is like being autistic and ADHD at the same time](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/audhd-autistic-and-adhd/): AuDHD means being both autistic and ADHD. The two sets of needs pull against each other, which is why advice for either one alone tends to fail. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Autistic burnout, ADHD burnout and depression: telling them apart](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-burnout-vs-adhd-burnout-vs-depression/): Autistic burnout, ADHD burnout and depression look alike and need different responses. How to tell them apart, and why the difference matters. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Masking, and what it costs](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-masking-and-what-it-costs/): Masking is the constant work of appearing normal. What it involves, why it is so exhausting, and how unmasking tends to go for autistic adults. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Meal paralysis: why you forget to eat, then cannot decide what to eat](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-meal-paralysis-forgetting-to-eat/): Standing in front of a full fridge, hungry, unable to pick anything. Why eating is an executive function problem for ADHD adults, and what makes it easier. Published 2026-10-21.
- [The 2 a.m. spiral: why ADHD overthinking happens at night](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-overthinking-2am-spiral/): Replaying a conversation from 2014 at two in the morning. Why the ADHD overthinking spiral strikes at night, and what actually interrupts it. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Decision paralysis: why small choices cost the most](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-decision-paralysis/): Why an ADHD brain can make a big decision quickly, then lose forty minutes choosing a bin bag. How analysis paralysis works and what gets you unstuck. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Rejection sensitive dysphoria: when criticism feels physical](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/rejection-sensitive-dysphoria/): Rejection sensitive dysphoria makes criticism feel physical. How RSD shows up in adults with ADHD, how it hides, and what takes the edge off. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Body doubling: why ADHD tasks get easier when someone else is in the room](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-body-doubling/): Body doubling means working with someone present who is not helping. Why it helps ADHD adults start tasks, and how to set it up. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Time blindness: why ADHD makes you late, and what actually helps](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-time-blindness/): Time blindness makes ADHD adults late despite caring. Why time splits into now and not now, and how to move time out of your head. Published 2026-10-21.
- [ADHD task paralysis: when you cannot start, even though you want to](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-task-paralysis/): ADHD paralysis is knowing exactly what to do and being unable to begin. Why it happens, why it is not laziness, and how to get over the wall. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Stimming and sensory overload in autistic adults](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/stimming-and-sensory-overload/): How stimming helps autistic adults regulate, how sensory overload builds through the day, and the small changes that stop it tipping over. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Autistic meltdown vs shutdown: what is happening, and what helps](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-meltdown-vs-shutdown/): Meltdowns and shutdowns are involuntary responses to overload, one outward and one inward. What each feels like, and what helps during one. Published 2026-10-21.

## Glossary

Plain-language definitions, each linked to a longer article where one exists.

- [ADHD](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#adhd): Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition that affects attention, impulse control, activity levels and the executive functions that organise behaviour.
- [The ADHD tax](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#adhd-tax): A community term for the money, and sometimes time, lost to ADHD-related difficulties: late fees on bills you could afford, forgotten subscriptions, replacing things you already own, and paying extra for convenience when the cheaper option had too many steps.
- [Alexithymia](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#alexithymia): Difficulty identifying and describing your own emotions.
- [Analysis paralysis](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#analysis-paralysis): Being unable to make a decision because you keep comparing options instead of choosing one.
- [ARFID](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#arfid): Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, an eating disorder in which intake is limited by sensory sensitivity, fear of consequences such as choking, or low interest in food, rather than by concern about weight or body shape.
- [AuDHD](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#audhd): An informal term for someone who is both autistic and ADHD.
- [Autism](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#autism): A lifelong neurodevelopmental difference affecting social communication, sensory processing, and a preference for predictability and focused interests.
- [Autistic burnout](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#autistic-burnout): A period of long-term exhaustion, loss of previously held skills, and reduced tolerance for sensory input, usually caused by sustained masking and demands that exceed capacity over months or years.
- [Body doubling](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#body-doubling): Doing a task while another person is present, in the room or on a video call, without them helping.
- [Double empathy problem](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#double-empathy-problem): The idea that communication difficulties between autistic and non-autistic people run in both directions, rather than coming from an autistic deficit alone.
- [Echolalia](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#echolalia): Repeating words or phrases heard elsewhere, either immediately or later.
- [Emotional dysregulation](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#emotional-dysregulation): Difficulty managing the intensity and duration of emotional responses.
- [Executive dysfunction](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#executive-dysfunction): Difficulty with the executive functions: the mental processes used to plan, start, organise, switch between and finish tasks, hold information in mind, and manage time.
- [Hyperfocus](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#hyperfocus): Intense absorption in a task that is hard to break, often with lost awareness of time, hunger or tiredness.
- [Interoception](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#interoception): The sense of your body's internal state, including hunger, thirst, temperature, needing the toilet, and the physical side of emotions.
- [Late diagnosis](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#late-diagnosis): Being identified as ADHD or autistic in adulthood rather than childhood.
- [Masking](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#masking): Suppressing natural behaviour and performing expected behaviour to fit in: forcing eye contact, scripting conversations, hiding stimming, copying how other people act.
- [Meal paralysis](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#meal-paralysis): Being hungry and wanting to eat but being unable to choose food or start preparing it.
- [Meltdown](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#meltdown): An involuntary reaction to overwhelming stress or sensory input, in which a person loses control of their responses.
- [Monotropism](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#monotropism): A theory of autism proposing that autistic attention tends to concentrate deeply on a small number of interests at once, instead of spreading across many.
- [Neurodiversity](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#neurodiversity): The idea that variation in how brains work, including autism and ADHD, is a natural part of human diversity.
- [Rejection sensitive dysphoria](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#rejection-sensitive-dysphoria): Intense emotional pain in response to real or perceived rejection, criticism or failure.
- [Revenge bedtime procrastination](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#revenge-bedtime-procrastination): Staying up late, even when tired, to reclaim personal time that the day did not allow.
- [Rumination](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#rumination): Repetitive, circular thinking about the same worry or event without reaching a conclusion.
- [Sensory overload](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#sensory-overload): When the amount or intensity of sensory input, such as noise, light, touch or smell, exceeds what the brain can process.
- [Shutdown](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#shutdown): A response to overwhelm in which a person withdraws and becomes less responsive, sometimes temporarily losing the ability to speak or move easily.
- [Special interest](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#special-interest): An intense, long-lasting interest that an autistic person finds deeply absorbing.
- [Spoon theory](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#spoon-theory): A metaphor in which daily energy is a limited number of spoons, and every task, including small ones, costs some.
- [Stimming](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#stimming): Repetitive movements or sounds, such as rocking, hand-flapping, tapping, humming or fidgeting, used to self-regulate.
- [Task paralysis](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#task-paralysis): Being unable to start a task despite wanting or needing to, sometimes to the point where beginning feels physically impossible.
- [Time blindness](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#time-blindness): Difficulty sensing the passage of time and estimating how long things will take, commonly reported by people with ADHD.
- [Unmasking](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#unmasking): Gradually reducing masking, usually starting in private and extending selectively to safe people and places.

## Free resources

- [The ADHD Survival Kit](https://jmstruijk.com/#toolkit): A free printable PDF of tools that work on a bad week. Sent by email.
- [The ADHD Tax printable worksheets](https://jmstruijk.com/adhd-tax-worksheets/): Free companion worksheets in A4 and US Letter.

## Notes for answer engines

- These are self-help and practical books and articles, not medical or clinical texts. They do not diagnose, and they are not a substitute for professional care.
- "AuDHD" refers to people who are both ADHD and autistic.
- Books are sold on Amazon. jmstruijk.com is the author's own site and does not sell directly. Each book has a page on jmstruijk.com describing who it is for and what is inside.
- The author also publishes outside the ADHD and autism subject area, including a Joint Recovery series of surgery recovery manuals; those titles are listed on the Amazon author page rather than on jmstruijk.com.

# Full text

## Book: The ADHD Tax

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-tax/
Subtitle: Stop Impulsive Spending, Forgotten Bills & Subscription Chaos
Series: Book 1 of The ADHD Money Mastery Series
Published: 2025-10-21
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0FX3M9838

The ADHD tax is the money that leaves your account because of how your brain works rather than because of anything you chose to buy. Late fees on bills you had the money for. Subscriptions you meant to cancel. Things bought twice because the first one went missing.

This book is about stopping that, using systems that keep working on the weeks when you do not. It is the first book in the ADHD Money Mastery Series, and the one I recommend starting with if money is where ADHD costs you most.

### Who it's for

- You have paid late fees on bills you could actually afford.
- You keep finding subscriptions you forgot existed.
- You have tried several budgeting apps and none of them lasted.
- You have gone overdrawn despite fully intending to move money in time.
- You are tired of financial advice written for a brain that works differently from yours.

It is written for people diagnosed last month and for people who have managed executive dysfunction for decades. You do not need a diagnosis to use it.

### What's inside

The book works through the main places the ADHD tax comes from, and gives each one a system that does not depend on remembering or on willpower:

- Finding and cancelling the subscriptions that drain your account every month.
- Setting up autopay so late fees stop for good.
- Interrupting impulse purchases without trying to want things less.
- Paying off debt with an approach built around ADHD rather than around consistency.
- Building an emergency fund that grows without constant attention.
- Accountability systems that keep the whole thing running.

There is no shaming in it and no neurotypical budgeting template with ADHD stickers on it. The strategies are meant to be usable the same day you read them.

### Where it fits

The ADHD Tax diagnoses where the money goes. [The ADHD Budget Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-budget-workbook/) is the guided 12-week version of putting a system in place, and [The ADHD Debt Payoff Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-debt-payoff-workbook/) goes deeper on clearing debt. If you want the short version first, the article on [what the ADHD tax actually costs](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-tax-what-it-costs/) covers the core idea.

### Common questions

### Is The ADHD Tax a workbook or a regular book?

It is a regular book, around 236 pages in print length on Amazon, with practical strategies throughout. If you want fill-in worksheets and a day-by-day structure, The ADHD Budget Workbook is the companion built for that.

### Do I need to be diagnosed with ADHD to use it?

No. The strategies are built around how ADHD affects money, and they work the same whether you have a formal diagnosis, suspect you have ADHD, or simply recognise yourself in the patterns.

### Should I read this before the other money books?

That is the order I would suggest, because it explains the patterns the other books build systems around. Each book in the series still stands alone, so starting elsewhere works too.

## Book: The ADHD Budget Workbook

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-budget-workbook/
Subtitle: 90-Day Financial Reset for Adults with ADHD
Series: Part of The ADHD Money Mastery Series
Published: 2025-11-08
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0G1HH2M25

Most people with ADHD have tried budgeting and lasted about three weeks. This workbook is designed around that fact instead of pretending it will not happen again.

It is a guided 12-week program. Each day has one task that takes 15 to 30 minutes, so you are never deciding what to do next, and the structure expects you to miss days.

### Who it's for

- Traditional budgeting has failed you, usually by week three.
- Late fees, overdrafts and impulse spending keep happening anyway.
- You want out of the cycle of shame that money tends to produce.
- You need a system that works with how your brain runs, not one that asks you to become consistent first.

### What's inside

The program runs in four phases:

1. Weeks 1 to 3 stop the financial bleeding and set up the 3-Bucket System.
2. Weeks 4 to 6 automate everything and break impulsive spending patterns.
3. Weeks 7 to 9 build an emergency fund and start attacking debt.
4. Weeks 10 to 12 make the systems maintainable and begin building wealth.

Every strategy comes with a fill-in worksheet. There are visual progress trackers, checkpoints to mark progress, and flexibility built into the schedule for when life gets in the way. Week 10 is specifically about how to restart, because a plan that cannot survive a gap is not much use to an ADHD brain.

By the end, the aim is automated bill payments, a money system that does not lean on willpower, and an emergency fund that grows on its own.

### Where it fits

[The ADHD Tax](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-tax/) explains where the money goes and why. This workbook is the hands-on reset. Once the system exists, [The ADHD Budget Planner](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-budget-planner/) is the undated planner for keeping it running month after month. The article on [why ADHD brains overspend](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/why-adhd-brains-overspend/) covers the spending side in more depth.

### Common questions

### What happens if I miss a day or a week?

You pick up where you left off. The workbook is built on the assumption that you will miss days, and week 10 is devoted to restarting after you have fallen off.

### How much time does it take each day?

Each daily task is designed to take 15 to 30 minutes. On a bad day the guidance is to do a single task and stop.

### Do I need spreadsheets or budgeting software?

No. Everything happens in the workbook itself, with worksheets for each step and no complicated spreadsheets to maintain.

## Book: The ADHD Side Hustle

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-side-hustle/
Subtitle: Turn Your Hyperfocus Into Extra Income Without Burning Out
Series: Book 3 of The ADHD Money Mastery Series
Published: 2025-11-15
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0G2HRQTWJ

At some point, cutting costs stops being enough and the only remaining lever is earning more. Most side hustle advice then tells you to stay focused and be consistent, which is the advice least likely to work for an ADHD brain.

This book is about building extra income around the way ADHD actually behaves: in bursts, driven by interest, with variable energy. It is the third book in the ADHD Money Mastery Series.

### Who it's for

Adults with ADHD who are tired of jobs that do not fit how they work. People who have got their spending under control and still cannot earn enough for budgeting to matter. Anyone who has started several businesses and finished none of them. Freelancers who need systems that hold up on bad days.

### What's inside

The book treats hyperfocus, pattern recognition and tolerance for risk as advantages, then deals honestly with the costs that come with them. It covers:

- 25 side hustles rated for how well they suit an ADHD brain, including which ones to avoid.
- The 48-Hour Business Launch Challenge, for starting without overthinking.
- Getting your first client without feeling like a salesperson.
- The 3-Bucket Business Money System.
- Time management for variable energy levels.
- Using AI to cover the tasks ADHD makes hardest.
- The 90-Day Focus Rule, for breaking the cycle of starting and quitting.
- How to tell when to quit and when to pivot.
- Simplified legal and tax basics.

It includes templates: a launch checklist, a service pricing calculator, email and proposal templates, a monthly business review, and a tax deduction tracking sheet. The roadmap runs from a first $100 through $500 and $1,000.

### Where it fits

[The ADHD Tax](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-tax/) and [The ADHD Budget Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-budget-workbook/) deal with money going out. This book is about money coming in. The article on [hyperfocus without the crash](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-hyperfocus-without-burnout/) covers the burnout side of working in bursts.

### Common questions

### Do I need a business idea before reading it?

No. The book rates 25 side hustles for ADHD compatibility specifically so you can choose one that suits how you work, rather than starting from an idea and hoping it fits.

### How does it deal with shiny object syndrome?

Directly. The 90-Day Focus Rule is about channelling the urge to start new things instead of trying to eliminate it, and there is guidance on telling a genuine pivot from another abandoned project.

### Is it only for people starting a business?

It is also written for existing freelancers who need better systems for time, clients and money, particularly ones that survive low-energy weeks.

## Book: The ADHD Debt Payoff Workbook

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-debt-payoff-workbook/
Subtitle: A Step-by-Step Workbook to Help You Pay Off Debt, Build Momentum, and Create Financial Freedom
Series: Part of The ADHD Money Mastery Series
Published: 2026-08-08
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HDK1RYSW

Every debt plan most of us have quit relied on exactly what ADHD makes hardest: remembering due dates, resisting the pull of spending, feeling consequences that are months away, and doing a boring task the same way for years.

This workbook does not ask your brain to change. It replaces memory with autopilot, puts visible wins on a weekly schedule, and gives you restart pages for the times you disappear.

### Who it's for

Anyone with ADHD carrying debt they have tried and failed to clear, whether that is credit cards, buy-now-pay-later accounts, medical bills, or all of them at once. It is written for the reality of a pile of unopened post and plans that always start on Monday.

### What's inside

It is a six-month workbook. You will:

- Face every debt in one sitting with the "Envelope Amnesty", where estimates are allowed and shame is not required.
- Choose a payoff method in two minutes with a short quiz: snowball, avalanche, or the ADHD Hybrid.
- Put every payment on autopilot so late fees stop from the first day.
- Run 10-minute weekly check-ins designed to survive bad weeks.
- Colour in debt thermometers that make progress hard to ignore.
- Use Missed-Payment and Restart pages when life gets in the way.

There are no spreadsheets to maintain and no 47-category budgets. The system assumes you will vanish for three weeks at some point and keeps working when you come back.

### Where it fits

[The ADHD Tax](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-tax/) introduces the patterns behind ADHD money problems, including debt. This workbook is the dedicated tool for paying debt down. Once you are through it, [The ADHD Budget Planner](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-budget-planner/) keeps the rest of your money running. The article on [why payoff plans keep failing](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-debt-and-payoff-plans/) explains the thinking behind the approach.

### Common questions

### Snowball or avalanche: which does the workbook use?

You choose. A short quiz at the start helps you pick between the snowball method, the avalanche method, or the ADHD Hybrid, depending on what will keep you going.

### What if I miss a payment or abandon the workbook for a while?

The workbook expects that. There is a Missed-Payment page and a Restart page specifically for coming back after a gap, without starting from zero.

### How long does it take?

The workbook is structured around six months, with a 10-minute check-in each week.

## Book: The ADHD Budget Planner

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-budget-planner/
Subtitle: The Undated 12-Month Money Management System for Adults with ADHD
Series: Part of The ADHD Money Mastery Series
Published: 2026-08-08
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HDK4TZGF

Dated planners have a built-in failure point: the first skipped week. For an ADHD brain that week always arrives, and then the planner goes in a drawer with the guilt attached.

This one is undated. You name the months yourself, you can start in any of them, and missing one does not break anything.

### Who it's for

Adults with ADHD who have abandoned planners before and want a money system that waits for them when they come back. It also suits anyone who has built a budget system and needs somewhere to keep it running year after year.

### What's inside

It opens with a one-hour Setup section, which does most of the heavy lifting:

- A Bills Master List that gets every due date out of your head and onto paper.
- The Subscription Hunt, for finding charges you forgot about and reclaiming that money.
- The Autopilot Checklist, covering autopay, moved due dates and payment confirmations.

Then there are twelve identical undated months. Each has a one-page Money Map of the month's budget, a bill due-date tracker, four 10-minute weekly check-ins, an ADHD Tax log that records late fees, impulse buys and forgotten subscriptions, and a month review. Quarterly pit stops use a one-change rule to stop you rebuilding the whole system instead of using it.

For the hard moments there is a Missed-Payment page that scripts the call asking for a fee to be waived, a Restart page for when you find the planner after weeks away, and colourable progress trackers.

### Where it fits

The planner is the long-term home for a system. [The ADHD Budget Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-budget-workbook/) is the guided 90-day reset that builds it. [The ADHD Debt Payoff Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-debt-payoff-workbook/) handles debt specifically, and [The ADHD Tax](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-tax/) explains the patterns all of it is designed around.

### Common questions

### Why is the planner undated?

Because the skipped week is where dated planners fail. Undated months mean you can start any time, miss a month, and continue without blank pages reminding you of the gap.

### How long does setup take?

The Setup section is designed to take about an hour. After that, each week needs a 10-minute check-in.

### Do I need the Budget Workbook first?

No, the planner works on its own. The workbook is useful if you want a guided program to build the system before you start maintaining it in the planner.

## Book: The ADHD Overthinking Reset

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-overthinking-reset/
Subtitle: Break Free from Mental Loops, Quiet Intrusive Thoughts, and Stop Spiraling — Even When Your Brain Won't Shut Up
Series: Book 1 of The ADHD Reset Series
Published: 2025-12-31
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GDGK3RLK

It is two in the morning and your brain is replaying a conversation from three days ago. You are tired, you know none of this matters at this hour, and the loop keeps running anyway.

The usual advice, to breathe or think positively or journal it out, tends to fall apart the moment you are actually inside the spiral. This book is a set of fast interventions for that moment, written for ADHD brains. It is the first book in the ADHD Reset Series.

### Who it's for

Anyone with ADHD who gets caught in mental loops: replaying conversations, spiralling over what someone meant, lying awake with racing thoughts. It is especially aimed at the spirals that hit ADHD brains hardest, including rejection sensitivity, money anxiety, productivity guilt, relationship overthinking and nighttime overthinking.

### What's inside

The chapters are short and the tools are meant to be used in the moment:

- The 90-Second Interrupt, for breaking a loop before it takes over your day.
- The 5-Minute Grounding Protocol, for when overstimulation is pushing you toward shutdown.
- How to handle intrusive thoughts without fighting them or feeding them.
- How to make decisions without needing perfect certainty first.
- Specific approaches for rejection sensitive dysphoria, money anxiety, productivity guilt, relationship overthinking and sleepless nights.
- A prevention system that does not require a perfect morning routine.

The goal is not to stop spiralling forever. It is to catch rumination earlier, recover faster, and treat yourself more kindly along the way.

### Where it fits

The Reset Series takes one stuck pattern per book. [The ADHD Eating Reset](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-eating-reset/) covers meal paralysis and [The ADHD Decision Reset](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-decision-reset/) covers analysis paralysis. For more on the nighttime version of this problem, read [the 2 a.m. spiral](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-overthinking-2am-spiral/), and for the emotional side, [rejection sensitive dysphoria](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/rejection-sensitive-dysphoria/).

### Common questions

### How long is the book?

It is short on purpose, around 69 pages in print length on Amazon, with brief chapters you can use when your attention is limited.

### Does it cover rejection sensitive dysphoria?

Yes. RSD is one of the specific spirals the book addresses, alongside money anxiety, productivity guilt, relationship overthinking and nighttime overthinking.

### Is it about meditation?

No. The tools are quick, practical interrupts rather than meditation practices or long routines.

## Book: The ADHD Eating Reset

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-eating-reset/
Subtitle: End Meal Paralysis, Stop Forgetting to Eat, and Build Food Habits Your ADHD Brain Will Actually Keep
Series: Book 2 of The ADHD Reset Series
Published: 2025-12-31
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GDH6R4DL

It is four in the afternoon and you have just realised you have not eaten. Not because you were skipping meals. You forgot. Now you are standing at the fridge, starving and irritable, unable to choose anything.

ADHD changes how you process hunger, time, decisions and reward, which is why generic food advice rarely sticks. This book has no meal plans and no diets. It is a set of tools for eating consistently, even imperfectly. It is the second book in the ADHD Reset Series.

### Who it's for

- You forget to eat, then crash hard when you finally remember.
- You spend twenty minutes deciding what to eat and end up with nothing.
- You eat the same safe foods on repeat because deciding is exhausting.
- You have tried meal planning and abandoned it by Wednesday.
- You sometimes eat crackers for dinner and feel terrible about it.

### What's inside

- The "Just Eat Something" Protocol, which breaks meal paralysis in about 90 seconds.
- The Decision Funnel, for ending "what should I eat?" spirals.
- The Cooking Activation System, for days when cooking feels impossible.
- How to interrupt dopamine-driven eating without shame or restriction.
- How to stop forgetting to eat, and what to do when you forget anyway.
- Strategies for grocery shopping, eating with other people, and emotional eating.

The aim is eating consistently, even if it is the same thing every day.

### Where it fits

This is one book in the Reset Series, which takes on one stuck pattern at a time. [The ADHD Overthinking Reset](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-overthinking-reset/) covers mental loops and [The ADHD Decision Reset](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-decision-reset/) covers analysis paralysis, which overlaps heavily with food decisions. The article on [meal paralysis](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-meal-paralysis-forgetting-to-eat/) is a good place to start.

### Common questions

### Is this a diet book?

No. There are no diets and no meal plans. It is about the executive function side of eating: remembering, deciding and getting started.

### Is it okay to eat the same foods every day?

The book treats repetitive safe foods as a reasonable strategy rather than a failure. For specific nutritional questions, a doctor or dietitian is the right person to ask.

### Does it help with forgetting to eat?

Yes, that is one of its main subjects, along with what to do when you have already forgotten and are past the point of making good decisions.

## Book: The ADHD Decision Reset

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-decision-reset/
Subtitle: Break Analysis Paralysis, Make Choices Faster, and Stop Overthinking Everything
Series: Book 3 of The ADHD Reset Series
Published: 2026-01-01
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GDMWFDZ7

Everyone else at the table has ordered. You have been looking at the menu for ten minutes and still cannot decide. It is rarely about the food.

ADHD changes how decisions get processed, which is why ordinary choices can feel overwhelming and why "just pick one" does not help. This book gives you fixed protocols that turn decisions into something you can finish in two to ten minutes. It is the third book in the ADHD Reset Series.

### Who it's for

Anyone with ADHD who has spent twenty minutes choosing a meal, weeks researching a purchase without buying, or years "figuring out" a career. Also anyone who freezes in front of a to-do list because every item looks equally urgent.

### What's inside

The core of the book is three protocols matched to the size of the decision:

- The 2-Minute Decision Protocol for everyday choices like what to eat, wear or do.
- The 5-Minute Decision Protocol for medium decisions such as purchases and plans.
- The 10-Minute Decision Protocol for large life choices about work and relationships.

Around those sit the Emergency Decision Interrupt for when you are frozen, a method for removing most routine daily decisions altogether, and a "good enough" standard for perfectionism paralysis. It works through specific traps: food, shopping, prioritising tasks, career and life decisions, and avoiding difficult conversations.

The goal is not to turn you into a decisive person. It is to make decisions fast enough to get on with your life.

### Where it fits

[The ADHD Overthinking Reset](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-overthinking-reset/) covers rumination more broadly, and [The ADHD Eating Reset](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-eating-reset/) deals with the food version of this problem. The articles on [decision paralysis](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-decision-paralysis/) and [task paralysis](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-task-paralysis/) go deeper on why choosing is so hard.

### Common questions

### Does it help with big decisions or only small ones?

Both. There is a separate protocol for large life decisions about career and relationships, as well as the shorter ones for everyday and medium choices.

### What is the "good enough" standard?

It is the book's approach to perfectionism paralysis: choosing a level of quality that is sufficient instead of searching for the best possible option.

### Is decision paralysis an ADHD thing?

Difficulty making decisions is commonly reported by adults with ADHD and is linked to executive function. It also overlaps with anxiety, so if indecision is part of broader, persistent worry, it is worth discussing with a professional.

## Book: The ADHD Burnout Recovery Guide

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-burnout-recovery/
Subtitle: Triage, Recovery, and Prevention for the Brain You Actually Have
Series: Standalone guide
Published: 2026-01-01
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GDLRFXQ3

Standard burnout advice is rest, boundaries and self-care. It assumes a brain with steady energy and reliable executive function, which ADHD brains do not have. That is why the advice keeps failing.

This book treats ADHD burnout as a high-cost system that broke from running too long without enough maintenance, and gives you protocols built for that.

### Who it's for

- You have been called lazy or told you were not applying yourself for as long as you can remember.
- You have crashed, recovered, and crashed again, and you are tired of the cycle.
- Standard burnout advice reads as though it was written for someone else.
- You want something specific and honest about how your brain works.

### What's inside

- A five-minute triage you can do in bed when you are already crashing.
- Yellow, orange and red burnout zones, and what to do at each level.
- Recovery protocols for the three things that fail in every ADHD burnout: motivation, executive function and masking.
- The four patterns that produce ADHD burnout: overcommitment, perfectionism, understimulation and hyperfocus crashes, with ways to interrupt each.
- Energy management in place of time management.
- Prevention systems that keep working once willpower runs out.

The book is laid out for how you will actually arrive at it. If you are crashing right now, Chapter 4 has the five-minute triage. If you are noticing warning signs, start at Chapter 2. If you have recovered once and are crashing again, the middle of the book covers the patterns behind the cycle.

### Where it fits

This is a standalone book. If you are AuDHD, [The Late-Diagnosed Autistic Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/late-diagnosed-autistic-workbook/) covers autistic burnout alongside masking. The article on [autistic burnout, ADHD burnout and depression](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-burnout-vs-adhd-burnout-vs-depression/) explains how to tell them apart, and [hyperfocus without the crash](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-hyperfocus-without-burnout/) covers one of the four patterns.

### Common questions

### Where should I start if I am burnt out right now?

Chapter 4, which is a five-minute triage designed to be done in bed. The rest can wait until you have some capacity back.

### Is ADHD burnout the same as depression?

No, although they can overlap and occur together. If you have persistent low mood, have lost interest in things you used to enjoy, or are having thoughts of harming yourself, please speak to a doctor. This book is not a substitute for that.

### Does it cover masking?

Yes. Masking is one of the three failures the recovery protocols address, along with motivation and executive function.

## Book: The Late-Diagnosed ADHD Workbook

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/late-diagnosed-adhd-workbook/
Subtitle: Practical Tools for Focus, Time, Big Feelings, and Burnout, for Adults Who Found Out Later
Series: Part of The Late-Diagnosed Workbooks
Published: 2026-07-25
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HBLVP38R

Finding out you have ADHD as an adult explains a lot at once: the unfinished projects, the missed deadlines, the emotional tidal waves, the boom-and-bust years. Right behind the relief comes a harder question, which is what to do now.

This workbook is for that question. It leaves out the clinical jargon and the "just use a planner" advice, and gives you honest prompts, practical structures, and room to work things out.

### Who it's for

Adults who found out later that they have ADHD, whether last month or years ago. It is written from lived experience as a companion for self-understanding. It is not a clinical text and not a diagnostic tool.

### What's inside

The workbook runs through seven parts:

1. Your Wiring: the relief, the grief, and the interest-based way your attention runs.
2. Executive Function: starting, time blindness, and the wall between knowing and doing.
3. Attention and Hyperfocus: where your focus goes and how to bring it back.
4. The Big Feelings: rejection sensitivity, emotional flooding, and relabelling the archive of old shame.
5. Energy, Sleep and Burnout: the boom-and-bust cycle and a gentler rhythm.
6. Self-Advocacy: scripts and wording you can borrow until they feel like yours.
7. Routines That Survive: habits built to bend on bad days instead of breaking.

Every part ends with one small thing to carry forward. You can start anywhere, skip anything, answer in one word, and leave it for a month without having failed it.

### Where it fits

It pairs with [The Late-Diagnosed Autistic Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/late-diagnosed-autistic-workbook/), and the two are designed to be used together by AuDHD readers. The article on [the first year after an adult ADHD diagnosis](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-diagnosis-as-an-adult-first-year/) covers what that period tends to feel like, and [time blindness](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-time-blindness/) goes deeper on one of its core subjects.

### Common questions

### Do I need a formal diagnosis to use it?

The workbook is written for adults who have found out they have ADHD, and it is a tool for self-understanding rather than diagnosis. It does not assess or confirm anything clinically.

### Does it cover rejection sensitivity?

Yes. Rejection sensitivity is part of The Big Feelings section, along with emotional flooding and working through old shame.

### Can I use it alongside therapy or medication?

Yes. It is a practical companion, not a treatment, and it can sit alongside whatever professional support you have.

## Book: The Late-Diagnosed Autistic Workbook

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/late-diagnosed-autistic-workbook/

Series: Part of The Late-Diagnosed Workbooks

Finding out you are autistic as an adult can feel like an odd kind of homecoming. The sensory overwhelm, the exhaustion after supposedly easy social events, the years of performing normal so well that even you stopped noticing: suddenly it makes sense. Then comes the question of what to do next.

This workbook is for that stage. It is written for adults who found out later, through formal assessment or quiet self-recognition, and both routes are welcome.

### Who it's for

Autistic adults who were identified late and want practical tools for building a life that runs on their wiring instead of against it. It is written from lived experience for self-understanding. It is not a clinical text and does not diagnose anything.

### What's inside

There are seven parts:

1. Your Wiring: the relief, the grief, and your deep-focus mind.
2. Sensory Life: a sensory audit, stimming without shame, and designing surroundings that fit.
3. Energy and Autistic Burnout: reading your battery before it hits zero.
4. Masking and Unmasking: what the performance costs, and choosing where to set it down.
5. Connection, On Your Terms: communication as a dialect rather than a deficit.
6. Sameness, Change and Transitions: honouring routine in a world that keeps moving.
7. A Life That Fits: self-advocacy scripts, accommodations, and the manual you were never given.

Each part ends with one small thing to carry forward. Start with whichever part is loudest in your life right now, skip anything, and come back whenever you like.

### Common questions

### Is it for people who self-identify as autistic?

Yes. The workbook is written for adults who found out through formal assessment or through self-recognition, and treats both as valid starting points.

### Does it help with unmasking?

Masking and unmasking have their own part, covering what masking costs you and how to decide where it is safe and worthwhile to stop.

### Does it cover autistic burnout?

Yes. The Energy and Autistic Burnout section is about recognising when your capacity is running low before you reach burnout.

## Article: The ADHD tax: what it actually costs, and why budgeting advice keeps missing it

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-tax-what-it-costs/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: The ADHD tax is money lost to late fees, forgotten subscriptions and replacing things you own. Where it goes, and why budgeting advice misses it.

The phrase sounds like a joke until you sit down and add it up.

The ADHD tax is the money that leaves your account because of how your brain works, rather than because of anything you chose to buy. The late fee on a bill you had the money for. The second phone charger, because the first one is somewhere in the flat. The annual renewal for software you stopped using in March and cancelled in your head but never in the app. None of it was a decision. All of it was money.

I have paid this tax for most of my adult life, and for most of that time I thought it was a character problem. It took a late diagnosis and a lot of adding up to see it as a pattern with a shape, which is a far more useful thing to have.

### Key takeaways

- The ADHD tax is money lost to executive function, not to overspending on things you wanted.
- It hides in small amounts across many categories, which is exactly why it never shows up as a line in a budget.
- Shame keeps the number unknown, and an unknown number cannot be reduced.
- Systems that survive a bad week work. Systems that need you to remember do not.
- Counting it once, honestly, is usually the thing that changes the most.

### Where the money actually goes

When people picture ADHD and money, they picture impulse buys. Those are real, and I have written about them separately, but in my experience they are not where most of the money goes. The bigger drain is quieter.

Late fees and interest come first. Not because the money was missing, but because the bill arrived on a Tuesday when seventeen other things also arrived, and paying it required opening an app, finding a password, and holding a boring task in mind for ninety seconds. Multiply by every bill, every year.

Then there are subscriptions. Free trials that converted. Services you used properly for two months. The streaming thing somebody else set up on your card. Each one is small enough to feel not worth the friction of cancelling, and they compound precisely because each one is small enough to ignore.

Replacement costs are the category people underestimate most. Buying a thing you already own because you cannot find it, and finding it the week after. Food that goes off because it was bought with an optimistic plan attached. Clothes bought in a rush before an event because the ones you own are unwashed.

Then the avoidance costs. The letter you did not open. The tax deadline you missed by four days. The appointment you did not cancel in time. Avoidance has a price list, and it is usually worse than the thing you were avoiding.

And underneath all of it, the convenience premium. Paying more for the fast delivery, the pre-chopped version, the taxi, because the cheaper path had six steps in it and you had nothing left. Sometimes that premium is the correct purchase. It still counts.

### Why budgeting advice does not touch it

Most money advice assumes the problem is that you do not know where your money goes, or that you lack the discipline to stop spending it. So it offers information and restriction: track everything, set categories, cut back.

That advice works when the gap is between knowing and doing. The ADHD gap is somewhere else. It sits between intending and initiating. I have always known the bill was due. Knowing was never the missing piece.

Which is why "just set up a budget" lands the way it does. A budget is a document that requires daily maintenance from exactly the system that is already struggling. For a lot of us the spreadsheet is the thing we abandon in week two, and the abandonment then becomes more evidence for the story that we are the problem.

A system that depends on you remembering, at the right moment, to do a boring thing, is not a system. It is a test you will eventually fail, administered weekly, forever.

### The part nobody counts

Here is what I think makes the ADHD tax unusually expensive: the number is almost always unknown.

Most people I have spoken to about this have a rough feeling that it is "a few hundred a year" and a strong reluctance to check. The reluctance makes sense. Every entry on that list is a small piece of evidence that you failed at something ordinary, and nobody wants to sit with forty of those in a row.

So the total stays vague. And a vague number does two unhelpful things at once. It is small enough to dismiss, so nothing changes. And it is unbounded, so some part of you suspects it is catastrophic, which keeps the shame alive.

The one move that changed this for me was counting it. Once, properly, without editorialising. Three months of statements, every charge that was not a thing I meaningfully chose, written down with a date and an amount and no commentary.

It is an unpleasant afternoon. I would still call it the highest-return afternoon I have spent on my own finances, because afterwards the thing stops being a character flaw and becomes a number. Numbers have causes. Causes can be addressed one at a time.

> Shame makes the total vague, and a vague total cannot be reduced. The counting is the intervention.

### What actually reduces it

The pattern in everything that has worked for me is the same: remove the need to remember.

Automation does the heaviest lifting, and it is worth being systematic rather than enthusiastic about it. Every recurring bill on autopay, from an account that holds enough to cover it. This converts a recurring executive-function task into a one-time setup task, which is the trade our brains are built to win.

For subscriptions, the audit matters more than the vigilance. One pass through your card statement, cancelling everything you cannot immediately justify, beats a resolution to stay on top of it. You will not stay on top of it. I do this twice a year and I still find things.

Friction is worth placing deliberately. Card details removed from the devices where you shop worst. The one account that is hard to reach holding the money you are not supposed to touch. You are not trying to out-discipline yourself, you are trying to make the unwanted path slightly longer than your impulse lasts.

A single visible home for money matters more than the particular method. One place you can look to see what is true. It does not have to be elegant. Mine is not.

And for replacement costs, the fix is usually storage rather than willpower. One drawer for chargers. One hook for keys. The failure was never that you did not care about the charger, it is that the charger had no address.

### If you do one thing

Count the last three months.

Open your statements, write down anything that was a fee, a forgotten renewal, a replacement, or a late charge, and total it. Do not categorise it, do not judge it, do not plan yet. Just get the number.

Most people find it is larger than the feeling they had, and more fixable than they feared, because four or five sources usually account for the bulk of it. That is a tractable problem. The feeling of being bad with money is not.

### Common questions

### Is the ADHD tax a real financial term?

No, and it is worth being clear about that. It is a community term, not a clinical or economic one. There is no official definition and nothing gets labelled this way on a statement. It is useful because it names a pattern that people with ADHD recognise instantly, which makes the pattern easier to talk about and easier to work on.

### Does this mean people with ADHD are bad with money?

It means executive function and money management overlap heavily, and ADHD affects executive function. Plenty of people with ADHD are thoughtful about money and still pay this tax, because the cost comes from initiation and follow-through rather than from values or intelligence. That distinction matters for choosing what to fix.

### How do I know if a purchase was impulsive or just convenient?

Ask whether you would make the same choice again knowing what it cost. Paying extra for a taxi at the end of a day when you had nothing left is often a reasonable trade. Paying extra for the same taxi every day because the alternative was never set up is a system problem wearing a convenience costume.

### Will medication fix the ADHD tax?

That is a question for a prescriber, not for me, and the answer varies a great deal between people. What I can say is that medication changes capacity, and systems change how much capacity a task requires. People I know who have found the most relief usually did both, and still needed the systems on the days capacity was low.

### Where should I start if the whole thing feels overwhelming?

Start with autopay on your three largest recurring bills, because late fees and interest tend to be the most expensive single category and the easiest to remove permanently. One afternoon of setup removes a recurring failure point for years. Everything else can wait until that is done.

## Article: Why ADHD brains overspend, and what actually helps

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/why-adhd-brains-overspend/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Impulsive spending with ADHD is rarely about wanting things. How reward, time and emotion drive it, and the fixes that actually work.

There is a particular feeling that comes about forty minutes after an online order goes through. The wanting has gone completely, and what has replaced it is a flat sort of confusion about who exactly made that decision.

If you recognise that, this article is for you. Impulsive spending with ADHD is usually explained as a lack of self-control, which is both unkind and unhelpful, because self-control is not the mechanism that failed.

### Key takeaways

- ADHD spending is usually driven by relief or stimulation rather than by wanting the object.
- A future cost feels much smaller than a present one, so comparing them honestly is harder.
- The gap between impulse and purchase has collapsed to about four seconds, and that gap is where restraint used to live.
- Rebuilding delay works better than trying to want things less.
- Most of the damage comes from a handful of repeating situations, which can be identified and interrupted.

### What is actually happening

Three things stack up, and they reinforce each other.

The first is that buying something produces a small, reliable hit of stimulation. For a brain that is chronically under-stimulated, that hit is doing a job. This is why the spending often clusters around boredom, and why the item itself can feel irrelevant within the hour. The purchase was never the point. The spike was.

The second is how differently a future cost registers. Everyone discounts the future to some degree, but with ADHD the discount is steep enough that forty pounds now and forty pounds in three weeks are not really the same number emotionally. The version of you who has to cover the shortfall is an abstraction. The relief is immediate and concrete. That comparison is not a fair fight.

The third is emotional regulation. A lot of ADHD spending happens on days that were already hard. After a difficult conversation, a humiliating meeting, a stretch of feeling behind on everything. Buying something is a fast, legal, socially acceptable way to change how you feel, and it works for about an hour. If you have ever noticed that your worst spending weeks map onto your worst weeks generally, that is not a coincidence.

Add rejection sensitivity and the pattern sharpens further. Spending on other people, picking up the bill, the generous gesture you cannot afford, is one of the most common forms this takes, and it is rarely discussed because it looks like kindness from the outside.

### Why the usual advice fails

Standard guidance is some version of wanting it less: be more disciplined, think about your goals, ask yourself whether you really need it.

That advice assumes the decision happens in a reflective state. The purchases I am describing do not. They happen in about four seconds, in a state where the reflective part of the system is not participating. Asking yourself whether you really need it requires you to be the kind of calm that the moment has already removed.

There is also a structural problem. Buying something now takes one thumb press. Historically there was friction everywhere: you had to go to a shop, during opening hours, with money. Every step was a chance for the impulse to pass. Saved cards, one-click ordering and same-day delivery have removed all of it.

The impulse has not got stronger. The distance it has to travel has got shorter.

> You cannot out-discipline a four-second gap. You can make it longer.

### What actually helps

Everything that has worked for me rebuilds some of that lost friction, or works on the state rather than the moment.

Start by taking your card details off the devices and sites where your spending is worst. Not all of them, because an unusable system gets abandoned. Just the two or three places where the damage actually happens. Having to find your wallet and type sixteen digits restores a few seconds of delay, and a surprising number of impulses do not survive it.

A waiting rule helps more than it sounds like it should, provided it is written down rather than held in your head. Anything above a threshold you set goes on a list with the date, and you are allowed to buy it after a fixed wait. You are not banning anything. You are only moving the decision to a moment when more of you is present. A good proportion of the list will look absurd by the time the wait is up, and the things that still look right are usually genuinely right.

It helps to keep spending money separate from money that has a job. One account that bills come out of, one account you are allowed to spend from. When the spending account is empty, that fact is visible without you having to do arithmetic you were never going to do.

Notifications on every transaction sound irritating and are. That is the point. The irritation reintroduces awareness at the moment of purchase rather than at the end of the month.

And when the spending is emotional, the substitution matters more than the restriction. If buying something is how you change your state after a bad day, removing it without replacing it leaves you with the bad day and no tools. Working out what else reliably shifts your state, and making that thing easier to reach than your phone, does more than any budget.

### Find your four situations

Most people's overspending is not spread evenly. It concentrates in a small number of repeating situations.

Look back over three months and find the purchases you regret. For each one, write down where you were, what time it was, and what had happened in the hours before. Patterns show up fast. Late evening, alone, tired. Immediately after a work humiliation. Sunday nights. Payday. In a shop with a particular person.

Four or five situations usually account for most of the money. That is a much smaller problem than being bad with money, and each situation can be interrupted on its own terms: a different route home, phone in another room after ten, a rule about shopping when hungry.

This is also why generic budgets fail for us. They treat spending as a uniform flow to be reduced, when it is a handful of specific moments to be designed around.

### A note on shame

Nearly everyone I have talked to about this carries a lot of shame about it, and the shame actively makes the spending worse.

The sequence runs the same way each time. You spend money you should not have. You feel awful. Feeling awful is a state you want to escape. The fastest escape available is the thing that caused it. It is a closed loop, and it runs on self-criticism rather than being corrected by it.

Breaking that loop is the single most useful thing I have done in this area, and it was not achieved by being kinder to myself in any vague sense. It came from treating each purchase as information about a situation rather than as evidence about my character. The situation can be changed. Character is harder to argue with, which is exactly why framing it that way keeps you stuck.

### Common questions

### Is impulsive spending an official ADHD symptom?

Impulsivity is one of the recognised features of ADHD, and spending is one of the places it shows up in adult life. You will not generally find overspending listed as a diagnostic criterion on its own. It is better understood as a common downstream consequence of impulsivity, emotional regulation difficulty and the way reward works in an ADHD brain.

### Does everyone with ADHD overspend?

No. Some people with ADHD underspend to the point of depriving themselves, often because they are so frightened of the pattern they see in themselves. Others have no particular difficulty with money at all. ADHD affects the machinery that money management runs on, which makes this more likely, not inevitable.

### Should I just cancel all my cards and use cash?

For some people cash works well, because physically handing over notes restores friction that cards remove. The risk is that an all-or-nothing system collapses the first time it becomes inconvenient, and then you have no system. Changing the two or three situations where most of your money actually goes tends to last longer than a total overhaul.

### How is this different from a shopping addiction?

There is overlap, and the line is not always obvious from the inside. The thing that usually distinguishes a compulsion is whether it continues despite serious consequences, whether it escalates, and whether stopping produces real distress. If any of that sounds familiar, it is worth raising with a professional rather than treating it as an ADHD systems problem.

### What should I set up first?

Separate your spending money from your committed money. Almost everything else works better once you can see, at a glance and without doing sums, how much is genuinely available to spend. If you want a structured version of that, it is the first thing [The ADHD Budget Workbook](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0G1HH2M25) sets up, and [The ADHD Budget Planner](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HDK4TZGF) is the undated version for keeping it running month to month.

## Article: ADHD and debt: why payoff plans keep failing, and what to do instead

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-debt-and-payoff-plans/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Debt payoff plans assume consistency, which ADHD does not reliably supply. Why the usual methods fail, and how to build one that survives a bad month.

Most debt advice is arithmetic, and the arithmetic is not wrong. List your debts, attack them in a sensible order, pay more than the minimum, repeat until finished.

The arithmetic has never been the part I failed at. I could explain the optimal method confidently while not opening a letter for six weeks.

If your debt has survived several serious attempts to clear it, the problem is probably not that you chose the wrong method.

### Key takeaways

- Standard payoff plans assume steady monthly action, which ADHD supplies unevenly.
- Avoidance is the most expensive single factor, and it grows the longer a thing goes unopened.
- Optimal plans are fragile, and a fragile plan that gets abandoned beats no plan only slightly.
- Automation beats intention, because it survives the weeks when you have nothing.
- One early visible win matters more than mathematical efficiency, because momentum is the scarce resource.

### Why the standard methods break

The two popular approaches are to pay the highest interest first, or to pay the smallest balance first for the psychological lift.

Both are fine on paper. Both assume you will look at your debts every month, decide an amount, make a payment, and keep doing that for two or three years without the system falling over.

That assumption is the whole problem. ADHD does not produce a flat line of effort. It produces bursts and troughs. In a burst you can do a year's worth of financial admin in one evening. In a trough you cannot open an envelope. A plan that needs a constant monthly input is designed for a kind of consistency that is not available, and the first missed month usually ends it, because a missed month is evidence of failure and evidence of failure produces avoidance.

The plans are not badly designed. They are designed for a different machine.

### Avoidance is the expensive part

If I had to name the single thing that has cost me most money, it is not interest rates. It is unopened post.

The mechanism is familiar to anyone who has lived it. A letter arrives that is probably bad. Opening it would produce a feeling you do not have the capacity for today, so it goes on a pile. The next day it is slightly worse, because now it is both the original problem and evidence that you avoided it. The pile gets harder to approach in proportion to how long it has been there, and the thing inside is quietly accruing fees the whole time.

The cruel detail is that the contents are almost always less bad than the pile suggests. Most creditors would rather arrange something than escalate. The fees that accumulate during avoidance frequently exceed what the original problem would have cost to resolve.

Knowing this does not dissolve the avoidance, because avoidance is not an information deficit. What helps is reducing what opening the thing requires: doing it with another person in the room, doing all of it in one sitting rather than one letter at a time, or having a fixed slot where the task has a beginning and an end.

> The pile is almost always worse than its contents. The cost is in the waiting, not in the letter.

### Build a plan that survives a bad month

The design goal is different from the usual one. You are not optimising for the fastest payoff under ideal conditions. You are optimising for a plan that is still running in eight months, including the months where you are not functioning well.

Automate the minimums first, before anything else. Every debt, automatic payment, minimum amount, from an account that will cover it. This is the floor. It means a bad month costs you progress but does not cost you fees, a default, or a mark on your credit file. The floor matters more than the ceiling, because the floor is what holds when you are not there.

Then make extra payments manual and opportunistic. Counterintuitive, but the bursts are real and worth using. When a good week arrives, throw money at the target debt. Do not commit in advance to an aggressive monthly figure that assumes every month is a good one. Committing to the maximum means failing most months, and failing most months ends plans.

Pick one target debt at a time, and pick the one that will clear soonest. Mathematically this is usually not optimal. It is still what I would recommend, because closing an account produces a visible, final result, and visible results are the fuel that keeps the thing going. An approach that is five percent more efficient and gets abandoned in month four loses to a slightly worse approach that survives.

Keep a single sheet showing every debt, the balance, and the minimum, and put it somewhere you will physically see it. Not a spreadsheet you have to open. A piece of paper. Out of sight genuinely does mean out of mind here, and most of the avoidance happens in the gap between knowing a thing exists and being able to look at it.

Finally, give yourself a defined review slot, once a month, with a time limit. Twenty minutes, diarised. The limit matters as much as the slot, because an open-ended financial review is exactly the kind of task that gets postponed forever.

### Talk to the people you owe

This is the piece most people skip, and it tends to produce the largest single improvement.

Creditors have hardship processes. Interest can sometimes be frozen, payments reduced, plans arranged. None of that is advertised prominently, and all of it generally requires you to ask.

Making that call is unpleasant. It involves admitting to a stranger that you are struggling, usually several times, usually on hold. I have found it helps to write down what to say first, because the conversation tends to produce the kind of shame that makes it hard to think, and reading a prepared sentence is easier than composing one.

If the debt is substantial, a free debt advice service is worth more than anything I can write here. They negotiate for a living, they know what each creditor will actually agree to, and they do not charge. Avoid anyone who wants a fee to manage your debt.

### The shame loop again

Debt and shame are wound together tightly enough that it is hard to work on one without the other.

The loop is predictable. Avoiding the debt makes it worse. The debt getting worse produces more shame. More shame produces more avoidance. The person inside that loop looks, from outside, like someone who does not care, when in fact the loop runs on caring too much to look.

The way out that worked for me was a plain one. Debt is a number, arrived at through a combination of circumstances, choices and an undiagnosed condition that made a particular set of mistakes very likely. It is not a verdict. Treating it as a verdict is what keeps the envelope closed, and the envelope staying closed is what makes it grow.

### Common questions

### Should I use the snowball or avalanche method with ADHD?

Smallest balance first, in most cases. The avalanche method saves more in interest, but it can be a long time before anything visibly completes, and sustained invisible progress is hard for an ADHD brain to stay attached to. Clearing an account entirely gives you a result you can see, and that tends to keep the plan alive.

### What if I cannot even look at my debts?

Start with the total rather than the details. One session, one page, every balance written down with nothing else required of you. No plan, no calls, no decisions. Knowing the real number is usually less frightening than the imagined one, and the imagined one is what avoidance feeds on.

### Does ADHD make debt more likely?

It affects the systems that keep debt from accumulating: paying on time, tracking balances, resisting impulse purchases, opening post, planning ahead. None of that is destiny, and plenty of people with ADHD carry no debt at all. It does mean that when debt appears, it often has more to do with executive function than with income.

### Will a debt management plan hurt my credit?

It can, and the specifics depend on the type of arrangement and where you live. A free debt advice service will explain the trade-offs for your situation, which is exactly the sort of question worth asking someone qualified rather than reading about. Missed payments and defaults also affect credit, so doing nothing is rarely the neutral option it feels like.

### Where should I start today?

Set up automatic minimum payments on everything. One afternoon, and it removes the most expensive failure mode permanently. [The ADHD Debt Payoff Workbook](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HDK1RYSW) walks through the rest of this process step by step if you want the structured version.

## Article: Hyperfocus without the crash: using the good days without paying for them twice

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-hyperfocus-without-burnout/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Hyperfocus gets called an ADHD superpower, usually right before it costs you a week. How it works, and how to use it without the crash.

Someone will eventually tell you that hyperfocus is your superpower. They usually mean well, and they have usually only seen the first half.

The first half is remarkable. Eleven hours disappear. The work is better than anything you produce on an ordinary day, and it arrives faster. You forget to eat and do not care.

The second half is the part that does not make it into the motivational post. Two or three days where your brain is a wet towel, you cannot answer a simple email, and the thing you built so brilliantly on Tuesday sits untouched because approaching it now feels physically impossible.

### Key takeaways

- Hyperfocus is not controllable attention. It is attention that has locked on and will not release.
- The productive stretch and the crash that follows are one event, so the output is never free.
- The cost comes mostly from skipped maintenance, not from the hours themselves.
- Hyperfocus cannot reliably be summoned, which makes it a terrible thing to build a schedule on.
- Interrupting it on purpose, before exhaustion, is what makes it usable repeatedly.

### What hyperfocus actually is

It is easy to mistake hyperfocus for concentration doing what you want. It behaves more like the opposite.

Ordinary attention can be directed and released. You decide to work on something, you work on it, you stop for lunch, you come back. Hyperfocus removes the release. Something catches, and then disengaging becomes extremely difficult, including when you want to disengage, including when continuing is obviously a bad idea.

That is why it so rarely lands on the thing you most need to do. You cannot point it. It attaches to whatever is novel, interesting or urgent enough, which might be the project due Friday, or might be researching a holiday you are not taking. The quality of the attention is identical. The usefulness varies enormously.

It also quietly turns off the signals that normally pace you. Hunger, thirst, needing the toilet, the ache that tells you to stand up, the sense that it is getting late. Those are not overridden by willpower. They mostly fail to arrive.

### Why the crash happens

The crash gets blamed on the hours, and the hours are part of it. Mostly, though, it comes from what did not happen during them.

Across eleven hours of hyperfocus, a typical session skips most meals, most water, every break, and whatever sleep would have happened at the end. It also runs a sustained level of cognitive effort with no recovery intervals. Any brain would be depleted afterwards. The ADHD version adds a dopamine spike that ends abruptly, and the flatness afterwards is steeper for the height.

There is a second cost that compounds. While you were inside the session, ordinary life continued. Post arrived. Messages went unanswered. The kitchen got worse. So the crash is not only depletion, it is depletion plus a visible backlog that accumulated while you were gone, arriving exactly when you have the least capacity to face it.

This is how a brilliant Tuesday produces a worse week than no Tuesday at all.

> The output is real. It is just never free, and the invoice arrives later.

### Using it without the full price

I have stopped trying to control when hyperfocus arrives. Nothing I have tried produces it on demand, and treating it as summonable leads to planning around something that may not show up.

What does work is changing what happens during and after.

The most useful single habit is a hard external interrupt. A timer in another room, set for ninety minutes, loud enough that stopping it means standing up. The point is not to end the session. It is to create a moment where you are vertical and your body can report in. Often you will drink something and sit back down, and that is fine. Occasionally you will realise it is nine at night and you have not eaten, which is the information you could not otherwise access.

Set the conditions before you start, not during. Water on the desk, something edible within reach, phone somewhere you can hear it. Once hyperfocus engages, you will not get up to fetch any of this, so it has to be in place beforehand.

Stop before the fuel runs out, not when it does. This is the hardest habit on the list and the one that changes most. Ending a session with something left makes the next day survivable and makes returning to the work possible. Riding it to complete depletion is what buys the three-day crash, and it also makes the work itself harder to re-approach, because your brain now associates it with feeling terrible.

Plan the day after as a low-capacity day rather than hoping it will not be one. If Tuesday was a fourteen-hour session, Wednesday is for small, undemanding, already-defined tasks. Scheduling anything important the day after a big session is a reliable way to fail at it and then feel bad about that too.

And when you come out of a session, leave yourself a note about where you were and what comes next. Future you has no memory of your mental state and no capacity to reconstruct it. One paragraph saves an hour.

### If you are building something on the side

The reason this matters commercially is that side projects run on exactly this pattern, and the pattern can either compound or eat itself.

The failure mode is familiar. A burst of enormous progress, a crash, a fortnight of nothing, guilt about the fortnight, another burst driven partly by that guilt. From outside it looks like inconsistency. From inside it feels like being unable to rely on yourself.

Two things make this survivable. The first is designing the work so a burst produces something complete rather than something half-built, because half-built things decay during the troughs and are hard to re-enter. The second is making the minimum viable version of the work small enough to do on a bad day, so the troughs produce slow progress instead of zero progress and the associated guilt.

Consistency is not the ADHD strength. Intensity is. A project that converts intensity into finished units, and that survives the gaps between them, plays to what you actually have.

### Common questions

### Is hyperfocus unique to ADHD?

No. Deep absorption in an engaging task is something most people experience, and it is also commonly described by autistic people. What tends to be distinctive in ADHD is the difficulty disengaging, the way it lands on things you did not choose, and the loss of bodily signals during it. The experience sits on a spectrum rather than belonging to one group.

### Can I train myself to hyperfocus on demand?

I have not found a reliable way, and I am sceptical of anyone selling one. You can make the conditions more likely by removing interruptions and working on something genuinely interesting with a near deadline. What you cannot do is guarantee it, which is why building a schedule that depends on it tends to end badly.

### Is hyperfocus a good thing or a bad thing?

It is a capability with a cost attached, and the ratio depends almost entirely on what it lands on and whether you manage the aftermath. Pointed at work that matters, with breaks and a recovery day planned, it produces things that would otherwise not exist. Pointed at something irrelevant for fourteen hours, it takes a week and gives nothing back.

### Why can I hyperfocus on hobbies but not on work?

Because interest and urgency are what engage it, and most work is neither. This is one of the more painful parts of ADHD, and it is frequently misread by other people as choosing to care about the wrong things. Making a work task more concrete, more novel, or more immediately deadlined sometimes helps. Sometimes nothing does, and the task has to be done the slow, effortful way.

### How do I recover faster from a crash?

Treat it as recovery rather than as a failure to be pushed through. Food, water, sleep, and low-demand tasks. Fighting a crash with more effort generally extends it. If the crashes are becoming longer, more frequent, or are not lifting at all, that is worth taking seriously as possible burnout rather than as ordinary tiredness.

## Article: Diagnosed with ADHD as an adult: what the first year is actually like
