URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-diagnosis-as-an-adult-first-year/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Relief, grief, and rereading your own life. What the first year after a late ADHD diagnosis tends to be like, and what helps.

Nobody warns you about the grief.

They warn you about the waiting lists and the paperwork and the possibility of being told no. Nobody mentions that a few weeks after you are told yes, you will be sitting somewhere ordinary, reconstructing a school report from twenty years ago, and find yourself genuinely upset about a child who was told to apply himself.

A late diagnosis is good news. It is also a specific kind of loss, and the two arrive together.

### Key takeaways

- Relief usually comes first, then grief, and the grief catches most people off guard.
- Rereading your own history is the main work of the first year.
- Telling people goes less well than you expect, and that is about them, not about you.
- Medication is a tool with a trial period, not a verdict on whether you are really ADHD.
- Most of the practical gains come later, once the emotional part has somewhere to sit.

### The first few weeks

The relief is enormous and slightly manic. There is a reason. There has been a reason the whole time.

Most people go through a phase of reading everything. Forums, books, videos, other people's accounts, usually at two in the morning. Every description lands. You keep finding sentences that seem to have been written about you specifically, and the recognition is a genuinely good feeling after years of not having a frame that fit.

There is often a burst of energy with it. Plans get made. Systems get bought. You are going to fix everything now that you know.

This phase is useful, and it is worth knowing that the plans made during it are usually too ambitious. Mine were. The energy is real, but it is partly the relief talking, and the relief does not stay at that level.

### Then the grief

It tends to arrive a few weeks or months in, often without warning, and the common reaction is to feel foolish about it. You got an answer. Why are you upset?

Because an answer is also a reframe of everything that came before it. The jobs you left. The friendships that went quiet because you did not reply for four months. The repeated, patient feedback that you had potential and were not applying it. The things people said about you that you accepted, because enough people said them that they looked like facts.

Rereading all of that with new information is the actual work of the first year, and it is heavier than anyone tells you. There is anger in it, often directed at people who should have noticed, which is complicated because they usually could not have. There is a specific sadness about the version of you who tried very hard at something that was never going to work the way it was being attempted.

Grief is the right word for it. It behaves like grief, it takes roughly as long, and it does not respond well to being hurried.

> You are not grieving a diagnosis. You are grieving the time spent explaining yourself with the wrong information.

### Telling people

This goes less smoothly than most people expect, and it is worth being prepared.

The responses that sting are rarely hostile. They are casual. Everyone is a bit ADHD these days. You seem fine to me. Isn't that just an excuse. You went to university, so it cannot be that bad. Most of these come from people who mean no harm and have no idea what they are dismissing.

A few things made this easier for me. Deciding in advance who actually needs to know, rather than announcing it generally while the relief is still high. Having one or two plain sentences ready, so you are not composing an explanation in the moment. And accepting that some people will simply not take it on board, and that their not understanding does not alter what is true.

Finding other late-diagnosed adults matters more than almost any other single thing here. Not for advice. For the specific relief of describing something strange and particular and having someone say yes, that, without needing it explained.

### Medication, if you go that way

This is a conversation for a prescriber, and the right choice differs enormously between people, so I will keep to what I can say honestly.

It is a trial, not a test. If the first thing does not work, or the dose is wrong, or the side effects are not acceptable, that is information rather than a verdict on whether your diagnosis was real. Plenty of people go through more than one option before finding something useful, and plenty decide against it entirely and do fine.

It also does not do what people imagine. The common description is a quieter head rather than a transformed life. Skills you never built do not appear because of a tablet. Systems still have to be built. What changes for many people is how much capacity there is available to build them.

### What helps in the first year

Go slower than the relief wants you to. The urge to overhaul everything in month one is strong and usually produces a pile of abandoned systems that then function as fresh evidence of failure.

Keep notes about yourself. Specific things you notice about how you work, when you crash, what sets off what. This is the raw material for every system you will build later, and you cannot reconstruct it afterwards from memory.

Choose one area and work on it for a season. Sleep, or money, or the thing that is currently doing the most damage. Not all of them at once.

Expect a flat period. A lot of people hit a dip around six to nine months in, when the explanation has stopped being new and the work of actually living differently has started. That dip is normal and does not mean the diagnosis was wrong or that you have wasted the opportunity.

And let the grief have room rather than trying to be grateful on schedule. It moves faster when it is allowed to happen than when it is argued with.

### Common questions

### Is it worth getting diagnosed as an adult?

For most people I have spoken to, yes, though for varied reasons. Some want access to medication. Some want workplace or study accommodations. Many want the explanation itself, which turns out to be worth more than expected. The main arguments against are cost, waiting times, and the fact that a diagnosis does not by itself change anything practical.

### Why was it missed when I was a child?

Commonly because childhood ADHD was understood more narrowly than it is now, and because the quiet, inattentive presentation does not disrupt a classroom. Children who were academically capable, or who masked well, or who were girls, were particularly likely to be overlooked. Being missed says something about the screening of the time rather than about the severity of your experience.

### Is late-diagnosis grief normal?

It is extremely common, and it is one of the least discussed parts of the process. Relief and grief coexisting is the usual pattern rather than a contradiction. If the low mood is persistent, deepening, or affecting your ability to function, that is worth raising with a professional, because late diagnosis also tends to surface things that were being managed by not looking too closely.

### How long does the adjustment take?

Most accounts I have encountered describe something like a year to feel settled, with the emotional work front-loaded and the practical gains arriving later. There is no schedule, and people who take longer have not done it wrong.

### What should I actually do first?

Nothing structural for a few weeks. Read, notice, write things down, and find other late-diagnosed adults. The systems work lands much better once the emotional ground has settled, which is why [The Late-Diagnosed ADHD Workbook](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HBLVP38R) starts with the rereading rather than with the productivity.

## Article: Finding out you are autistic in adulthood

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-in-adulthood-late-diagnosis/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: What changes when you find out in your thirties or forties that you are autistic, why so many adults are missed, and what the first months involve.

It rarely starts with a doctor. For most people I have spoken to, it starts with a video, or a thread, or a friend's offhand comment, and then a long quiet period of reading at night without telling anyone.

The first reaction is usually to dismiss it. You do not look autistic, by which you mean you do not resemble the narrow version you were shown growing up. You have friends. You can hold a conversation. You made eye contact with someone this week.

Then you read a description of sensory overload, or of what a social event costs afterwards, and something you assumed was universal turns out to be specific.

### Key takeaways

- Most late-identified autistic adults have been masking so long that the mask reads as personality.
- The old diagnostic picture missed anyone who was verbal, academically able, or socially motivated.
- Self-identification is widely accepted in autistic communities, and formal assessment is expensive and slow in many places.
- The first months are mostly reinterpretation, not change.
- Sensory needs are usually the fastest practical improvement available.

### Why you were missed

The description that most adults alive today were measured against was built from observations of young boys with obvious, visible differences. If you were verbal, did well at school, and wanted friends, you did not resemble that description and nobody looked further.

Masking is the other half of it. If you worked out early that copying other people produced better outcomes than being yourself, you got good at it, and the better you got the less anyone saw. Many late-identified adults were praised throughout childhood for exactly the behaviour that was concealing them. Being described as mature for your age, or sensitive, or a bit of an old soul, often turns out to mean something else in retrospect.

Women, non-binary people, and anyone who was socially motivated enough to study people deliberately were missed at much higher rates. So were people whose difficulties got filed under anxiety, depression, or an eating disorder, which were treated for years with limited effect because the underlying thing was never addressed.

### The reinterpretation

The work of the first months is not change. It is going back through your own history with a different lens.

The exhaustion after social events that you assumed was introversion and could never quite square with the fact that you liked the people. The specific clothing you have always bought, which you thought of as a preference and now looks like a sensory requirement. The jobs that went wrong for reasons you could never explain properly. The childhood interests that were so consuming other people found them strange, and which you learned to talk about less.

Food comes up for almost everyone. Textures, temperatures, the same meal for years, a short list of things that are safe. Most people had this filed under fussiness, usually because that is what they were told.

So does the lifelong sense of running a translation layer. Watching how others do things, copying it, checking the result, adjusting. Many late-identified adults describe realising that other people are not doing this, which is a genuinely disorienting thing to learn in your forties.

> The mask is not something you put on. By the time you find out, it is most of what you think you are.

### The part that is hard

The relief is real and it is not the whole story.

There is anger, often at the places that were supposed to notice. There is grief for the decades spent trying to fix things that were never faults. There is a specific loneliness in realising that the effort you have been making invisibly was both enormous and unacknowledged, because the entire point of masking was that nobody could tell.

Identity gets unstable for a while. If a large portion of your behaviour was learned camouflage, working out what is underneath takes time, and the question of who you would have been without it has no answer. It is worth sitting with anyway.

And there is an awkward practical problem. Once you know, the mask becomes harder to hold. Many people find their tolerance for environments they used to survive drops sharply after identification. That is usually interpreted as getting worse. It is more often the end of a very long unconscious effort, which is not the same thing.

### Assessment, if you want one

Whether to pursue a formal diagnosis is genuinely a personal decision, and the honest answer is that it depends on what you need it for.

Formal assessment can matter for workplace adjustments, educational support, and in some places access to services. It can also provide a certainty that self-identification does not, which matters to some people a great deal.

The costs are real. Long waits in public systems, significant expense privately, and clinicians who vary in how well they recognise adults who mask. Some people go through assessment and are told no by someone working from an outdated picture, which is painful and does not settle the question.

Self-identification is accepted in most autistic communities and is a legitimate position, particularly given that access to assessment is unevenly distributed. You do not need anyone's permission to understand yourself accurately.

### What helps early

Sensory changes give the fastest return. Loop earplugs or noise-cancelling headphones, lower lighting, clothing chosen for how it feels rather than how it looks, a room at home that is quiet and dim and nobody else's. These are small, cheap, and often make a noticeable difference within days, which matters when everything else is in flux.

Recovery time needs to be scheduled rather than hoped for. If a social event costs you a day, that day is part of the event, and planning as though it is not is how people end up in a deficit they cannot explain.

Stimming, if you suppressed it, is worth letting back in. Most late-identified adults were trained out of visible self-regulation young, and getting it back tends to help more than expected.

Reading autistic adults rather than clinical material is the other thing I would recommend without hesitation. The clinical literature describes autism from outside, in terms of deficits observable to other people. Autistic writers describe it from inside, and that is the version that is actually useful for living.

### Common questions

### Can you become autistic as an adult?

No. Autism is lifelong and present from early development. What happens in adulthood is recognition rather than onset. People frequently find, once they look, that the evidence was there throughout childhood and was interpreted as something else at the time.

### Is self-diagnosis valid?

It is widely accepted within autistic communities, particularly given the cost and waiting times for formal assessment and the number of adults turned away by clinicians working from an outdated picture. Formal diagnosis still matters for accommodations and services in many places. Both things can be true at once.

### What is the difference between being autistic and being introverted?

Introversion is about where your energy comes from and is one trait among many. Autism involves differences in sensory processing, communication, social intuition, and a need for predictability, and it is present across every part of life rather than only in social settings. Plenty of autistic people are sociable and still find socialising expensive in a way introversion does not explain.

### Why do I feel worse since finding out?

This is extremely common and usually reflects the end of unconscious masking rather than a decline. Once you know what you have been doing, holding it becomes harder, and the full cost of it becomes visible for the first time. Many people describe a period of reduced tolerance before things stabilise.

### Where do I start?

Sensory changes, because they are immediate and cheap, and reading autistic authors rather than clinical descriptions. [The Late-Diagnosed Autistic Workbook](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HBNKNWZC) is built around that order, starting with sensory needs and masking before anything else.

## Article: AuDHD: what it is like being autistic and ADHD at the same time

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/audhd-autistic-and-adhd/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: AuDHD means being both autistic and ADHD. The two sets of needs pull against each other, which is why advice for either one alone tends to fail.

For a long time these two were not allowed to coexist. Diagnostic rules in several countries actively prevented clinicians from recording both, which means a generation of people were given whichever label was noticed first and sent away with half an explanation.

That changed. Plenty of us had already spent decades finding that advice for one condition kept failing in ways that advice for the other would have predicted.

AuDHD is the informal term for being both. It is not two conditions sitting side by side, politely taking turns. The interaction produces something with its own shape.

### Key takeaways

- AuDHD is autism and ADHD together, and the two sets of needs frequently contradict each other.
- Advice written for either condition alone tends to fail, because following it worsens the other side.
- The contradictions can make people appear less affected than they are, which delays identification.
- Burnout tends to arrive harder, because both sets of demands are being managed at once.
- Designing for the conflict directly works better than picking a side.

### The contradiction

The central experience is wanting two incompatible things with equal sincerity.

One part of you needs routine, predictability, and sameness. The same meal, the same route, the same sequence, because deviation is genuinely costly. The other part is bored to the point of pain by exactly that sameness and will sabotage it for novelty.

So you build a beautiful system. It works. The autistic part relaxes into the structure, which is a real relief. Then around week three the ADHD part has had enough, the system becomes intolerable, and you abandon something that was working perfectly well for reasons you cannot defend.

This happens with food, with work, with sleep, with hobbies, with the layout of a room. It is the defining pattern.

Social life runs on the same fault line. You want contact and you want to be left alone, often within the same hour. Socialising is draining in the autistic way and sought out in the ADHD way, which produces a cycle of overcommitting, enjoying it, and then needing to vanish for a fortnight.

Planning is similar. A real need to know what is happening next, and a complete inability to reliably do the thing that was planned.

> The usual advice fails because it was written for one half. Follow it faithfully and you make the other half worse.

### Why it goes unnoticed

The two sides partially cancel out, which makes AuDHD people look more functional than they are.

The ADHD chaos is dampened by autistic systems and rule-following, so you are not as visibly disorganised as ADHD alone would predict. The autistic rigidity is softened by ADHD flexibility and distractibility, so you are not as visibly rigid as autism alone would predict. From outside, neither picture is complete, so neither gets investigated.

What shows up instead is cost. Anxiety, depression, exhaustion, a sense of working extraordinarily hard for ordinary results. Those get treated, sometimes for years, with mixed results, because the treatment is aimed at the smoke.

The other reason is sequencing. Many people get one diagnosis, work hard on it, and find that a stubborn remainder does not respond. That remainder is frequently the other condition. If you have been told you have ADHD and the ADHD strategies only partly work, or you have been identified as autistic and your life is still chaotic in ways autism does not explain, it is worth considering.

### What actually helps

The approach that works is designing for the conflict rather than pretending one side will eventually win.

Build structures with variety inside them. Fixed frame, flexible contents. A set meal time with a rotating set of options. A fixed working block where what you work on varies. This satisfies the need for predictability without triggering the boredom response, and it is the single most useful principle I have found.

Keep several systems in rotation rather than searching for the perfect one. Expect to abandon the current method every few weeks, and plan for the abandonment instead of treating it as failure. Two or three systems you cycle between will outlast one system you believe in.

Protect the non-negotiable sensory things absolutely, and let the novelty happen elsewhere. Sensory overload does not become more tolerable because the ADHD side wants excitement. Keep the environment stable and let the stimulation come from ideas, projects or people.

Make rest more specific than the word suggests. Autistic recovery usually means low sensory input and no demands. ADHD recovery usually means stimulation and novelty. Doing one when you need the other leaves you unrested, and most people have to learn to tell the difference deliberately, because both register vaguely as tiredness.

Shrink transitions wherever you can. Switching tasks is costly for the autistic side and the ADHD side both, for different reasons, which makes it unusually expensive for AuDHD people. Fewer, longer blocks beat a day full of context switches.

### About burnout

It is worth saying plainly that AuDHD burnout tends to be severe.

You are running both sets of demands at once. The masking, the sensory management, the social translation, plus the constant executive effort of initiating, remembering, and finishing. Each is tiring. Together they can consume everything without producing much that looks like output, which makes the exhaustion hard to justify to yourself or anyone else.

Recovery is slower than people expect, and it is frequently interrupted. The ADHD side gets bored of resting and starts a project, which delays the recovery the autistic side needed, which deepens the burnout. If you have never managed to rest properly through a burnout, that mechanism may be why.

### Common questions

### Can you have both autism and ADHD?

Yes, and it is common. Diagnostic rules in several countries previously prohibited recording both, which is why many adults were given only one. Those rules have changed, though clinical practice has not caught up everywhere, and some assessors still look for one at a time.

### Is AuDHD an official diagnosis?

No. It is a community term for having both autism and ADHD. You would be diagnosed with each separately, and no clinician will write AuDHD on a form. The word exists because the combination produces experiences that neither diagnosis describes on its own.

### How do I know if I am AuDHD rather than just one?

Usually through the contradictions. Needing routine and destroying it. Wanting people and needing to disappear. Being organised about some things in a way that looks obsessive and chaotic about others in a way that looks careless. If strategies for one condition keep making a different part of your life worse, that is the pattern worth looking at.

### Do the traits cancel each other out?

They mask each other from the outside, which is different from cancelling out internally. The effort of managing both continues regardless of how it appears. This is a large part of why AuDHD people are often identified late and are frequently told they seem fine.

### Where should I start?

With the conflict itself rather than with either condition separately. Work out which of your needs are sensory and non-negotiable, and which are about stimulation and can be moved. [The Late-Diagnosed ADHD Workbook](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HBLVP38R) and [The Late-Diagnosed Autistic Workbook](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HBNKNWZC) are written to be used together for exactly this reason.

## Article: Autistic burnout, ADHD burnout and depression: telling them apart

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-burnout-vs-adhd-burnout-vs-depression/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Autistic burnout, ADHD burnout and depression look alike and need different responses. How to tell them apart, and why the difference matters.

From the outside these three look close to identical. Someone who was managing is no longer managing. They are exhausted, withdrawn, not answering messages, and unable to do things they could do easily six months ago.

From the inside they feel different, and more usefully, they respond to different things. Treating autistic burnout as depression wastes months. Treating depression as burnout can be worse than wasting months.

I am not a clinician and this is not a diagnostic tool. It is the distinction I wish someone had drawn for me years earlier, because I spent a long time applying the wrong remedy with great determination.

### Key takeaways

- Autistic burnout comes from sustained masking and sensory demand, and it needs reduced input.
- ADHD burnout usually follows a long stretch of effortful overcompensation, often after a crash.
- Depression is a medical condition that can occur alongside either, and it needs professional support.
- Burnout generally lifts when demands drop. Depression generally does not.
- The presence of anticipatory pleasure is one of the more useful signals, though none of this is a substitute for assessment.

### Autistic burnout

This one builds slowly, often over years, and then arrives as a collapse that seems disproportionate to whatever immediately preceded it.

The characteristic features are a loss of skills you previously had. Speech becomes harder, and some people lose it temporarily. Things you could tolerate become intolerable: lighting, noise, texture, the radio in someone else's car. The mask stops working, and social interactions you used to manage competently become impossible to perform.

Executive function drops sharply. Cooking, washing, replying to anything. The capacity simply is not available.

What causes it is sustained demand without adequate recovery. Masking all day. Managing sensory input you cannot control. Meeting social expectations that require constant translation. None of it registers as work, which is why the exhaustion seems to come from nowhere, and why people experiencing it frequently insist they have no reason to be this tired.

What helps is subtraction. Fewer demands, less sensory input, more time alone, and permission to stop masking. Recovery is often measured in months, not days, and people underestimate this consistently. Pushing through, which is the response most of us learned, makes it substantially worse.

### ADHD burnout

The shape here is different. Less of a slow build, more of a repeated cycle that eventually fails to reset.

The pattern is overcommitting during a good stretch, working at an unsustainable intensity to compensate for the periods where nothing got done, hitting a wall, recovering partially, and starting again slightly more depleted. Run that for long enough and the recovery stops happening.

It usually comes with a heavy load of guilt and a backlog. Unfinished projects, unanswered messages, things you promised during an optimistic phase and cannot now face. The shame is a load-bearing part of this one, because it drives the next round of overcompensation.

Interest-based attention stops working, which is the sign most people find alarming. The things that normally engage you, that you could always rely on to pull you out, do not. That loss of the one reliable fuel source is distinctive.

What helps is reducing the number of open loops, finishing or formally abandoning things, and rebuilding smaller commitments that you can actually meet. Rest alone often does not fix it, because the backlog is still generating pressure.

### Depression

Depression is a medical condition, and I want to be careful here, because the distinction matters most in this direction.

The feature most often described as distinguishing is pervasive low mood and anhedonia: the absence of pleasure, including anticipatory pleasure. With burnout, people usually still want things. They want to rest, want to see a particular person, look forward to something, and simply have no capacity to act. With depression, the wanting itself is frequently gone.

Depression also tends to carry a view of the self rather than of the circumstances. Burnout says I cannot keep doing this. Depression says I am worthless. The second is a different kind of statement.

And crucially, burnout generally improves when the demands come off. Depression often does not improve when circumstances improve, which is one of the cruellest things about it.

If there is any possibility of depression, that is a conversation with a doctor rather than a self-management project. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact emergency services or a crisis line where you are.

> Burnout tends to lift when the demands drop. If the demands dropped and nothing lifted, that is worth taking to a professional.

### They overlap

The reason this is genuinely difficult is that these rarely arrive one at a time.

Prolonged autistic burnout frequently produces depression. ADHD burnout and depression share a large portion of their presentation. Someone who is AuDHD can be in both kinds of burnout simultaneously, which is a particularly confusing place to be, because the two call for opposite responses: one wants less input, the other is starved of stimulation.

This is a strong argument against self-diagnosis as a final answer. It is a reasonable argument for using these distinctions as a way to describe your experience accurately to someone qualified, which tends to produce better help than arriving with no language for it.

### What to do with the distinction

The practical value is in choosing the first move.

If it looks like autistic burnout, subtract. Cancel what can be cancelled, reduce sensory load, stop masking where it is safe to, and plan in months.

If it looks like ADHD burnout, close loops. Finish or formally drop the open commitments, reduce what you agree to going forward, and address the backlog that is generating the pressure.

If anything suggests depression, particularly absent anticipatory pleasure, persistent hopelessness, or a change in how you see yourself rather than your circumstances, make an appointment. The self-management approaches are not a substitute and the delay is costly.

And if you are AuDHD and both are present, subtract first. The sensory and masking load has to come down before anything else is workable, and attempting the stimulation-based fixes while still overloaded generally fails.

### Common questions

### Is autistic burnout an official diagnosis?

No. It is a well-described experience in autistic communities and has been the subject of research, but it does not appear as a formal diagnostic category. That means clinicians vary a great deal in whether they recognise it, which is one reason many autistic adults are treated for depression first.

### How long does autistic burnout last?

Accounts vary widely, from weeks to well over a year, and the length depends heavily on whether the demands causing it actually come down. Recovery that keeps being interrupted by a return to the same load tends to extend indefinitely. This is one of the main reasons it is so often underestimated.

### Can you have burnout and depression at once?

Yes, and it is common, particularly when burnout has gone on a long time. Having one does not rule out the other, which is a good reason to involve a professional rather than deciding between them yourself.

### Why does rest not fix my ADHD burnout?

Usually because the pressure is not only depletion. Unfinished commitments, unanswered messages and unmet promises keep generating load whether you are resting or not. Many people find that closing or formally abandoning open loops does more than additional sleep.

### What is the first thing to do?

Reduce the demand that is actually causing it, which means working out which kind you are in. If you cannot tell, or if the low mood is persistent, start with a doctor. [The ADHD Burnout Recovery Guide](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GDLRFXQ3) covers the triage version of this in more depth.

## Article: Masking, and what it costs

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-masking-and-what-it-costs/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Masking is the constant work of appearing normal. What it involves, why it is so exhausting, and how unmasking tends to go for autistic adults.

Masking is the work of appearing normal, and the people doing most of it are usually the least aware of it.

It is not a performance you decide to give. For most late-identified adults it was assembled in childhood out of trial and error, kept because it worked, and run so continuously that it stopped being distinguishable from personality. You cannot drop something you do not know you are holding.

The usual way people find out is by noticing the cost first, and working backwards.

### Key takeaways

- Masking is suppressing natural behaviour and performing expected behaviour, usually automatically.
- It is effortful in a way that does not register as effort, which is why the exhaustion seems unexplained.
- It works, which is precisely why it is so hard to give up.
- It is strongly associated with burnout, anxiety and depression in autistic adults.
- Unmasking is gradual and situational, and safety has to come first.

### What it actually involves

Masking is made of small, constant adjustments.

Rehearsing conversations in advance, including ones that will probably not happen. Monitoring your face in real time to check it is doing the right thing. Making eye contact at measured intervals because you learned the interval, counting rather than feeling it. Suppressing the movement your body wants to make: the rocking, the hand movements, the tapping, usually replaced with something less visible like a foot or a thumb against a finger.

It involves copying. Many late-identified adults describe having assembled a personality out of pieces of other people, sometimes consciously, often from television. Laughing a beat after everyone else because the laugh is a response to the group rather than to the joke. Having scripts for ordinary interactions and panicking when a conversation leaves the script.

It also means hiding what you actually care about. Learning that your interests are too much, so you ration how long you talk about them and watch the other person's face for the point where you should stop.

None of this is dishonesty. It is accommodation, performed unilaterally, usually without acknowledgement.

### Why it is so expensive

The cost comes from the fact that it never stops and never becomes free.

Most skills become automatic and cheap with repetition. Masking stays expensive because it requires continuous real-time monitoring. You are running the conversation and simultaneously running a process that checks your own output against a model of what is expected. That second process is the load, and it runs for the entire duration of every social interaction.

On top of that, suppressing stimming removes your main regulation tool at exactly the moment you need it. Stimming is how many autistic people manage sensory and emotional load. Masking means holding that load with the regulator switched off.

The bill arrives afterwards, which is why it is hard to connect to its cause. You were fine at the event. You were fine on the way home. Then you are flat for two days and it looks like nothing happened, because from outside nothing did.

Sustained over years, this is one of the main routes into autistic burnout. It is also associated with anxiety and depression, and with a particular kind of loneliness: being surrounded by people who like a version of you that you built and maintain at considerable expense.

> People liking the mask is not the same as being known, and the gap between those two is where the loneliness lives.

### Why people keep doing it

Masking works. That has to be said plainly, because advice to simply stop tends to come from people who have not weighed what stopping costs.

It gets you employed. It gets you through interviews, meetings and performance reviews. It keeps you safe in environments where visible difference attracts hostility. For many people it has been the thing standing between them and much worse outcomes.

So it is not a bad habit. It is a strategy that was correct at the time, that has a running cost, and that most people were never given the chance to opt out of. The question worth asking is not whether to mask, but where it is still buying you something and where you are paying for nothing.

### How unmasking tends to go

It is slower and more situational than the word implies, and it is not a single event.

It generally starts in private. Letting yourself stim at home. Wearing what is comfortable. Dropping the voice you use on the phone. Noticing, often with some surprise, how much quieter it is in your head without the monitoring running.

Then it extends selectively, usually with one or two people first. This is where most of the fear lives, and the fear is not irrational. Some relationships are built substantially on the masked version, and some of those do not survive. Most people find a smaller number of closer relationships on the other side, which is generally an improvement and does not feel like one at the time.

Work is usually last, and often partial. Plenty of people stay masked professionally and unmask everywhere else, which is a legitimate choice rather than a failure of commitment. Safety is a real consideration, and it is not evenly distributed.

A thing worth preparing for: it often feels worse before it feels better. Many people find their tolerance for masking drops sharply once they can see it. Environments you used to manage become difficult. That is usually the end of a very long unconscious effort rather than a deterioration, although it does not feel that way from inside.

### Where to start

Notice first, change nothing. Spend a week observing what you do in social situations. What you suppress, what you perform, what you rehearse. Most people are surprised by the volume once they look.

Pick the cheapest change. Something entirely private, with no social consequence. Stimming in your own home is the usual starting point, and the relief is often immediate and larger than expected.

Work out where masking is still earning its cost. Sometimes it genuinely is, and continuing is the right call. Sometimes you are masking out of habit in a room where nobody would mind, and that is the free ground.

Account for recovery honestly. If a masked event costs you a day, the event takes two days. Planning as though it takes one is how the deficit builds.

### Common questions

### Do only autistic people mask?

No. People with ADHD mask too, often hiding inattention, impulsivity or the effort of keeping up. Anyone whose natural behaviour has been treated as unacceptable may develop something similar. The autistic version is the most studied and tends to be the most comprehensive, covering social, sensory and communication behaviour at once.

### Is masking the same as being polite?

No, although the line can look blurry from outside. Everyone adjusts their behaviour by context. Masking is sustained suppression of natural behaviour and continuous performance of unnatural behaviour, running constantly, with a measurable cost afterwards. Politeness does not usually require two days of recovery.

### Should I stop masking at work?

That depends entirely on your workplace, your legal protections, and your financial position, and anyone who answers confidently without knowing those does not know enough. Many people unmask partially, in low-risk ways, and keep the rest. There is no obligation to be visible at your own expense.

### Why am I more tired since I found out I was masking?

Because awareness makes it harder to sustain, and because you can now see effort that was previously invisible to you. Most people describe a dip after identification before things improve. It usually reflects the cost becoming visible rather than increasing.

### How do I know who I am underneath it?

Slowly, and partly by elimination. It helps to notice what you do when nobody is watching, what you are drawn to when there is no social cost, and what you avoid when avoidance is free. [The Late-Diagnosed Autistic Workbook](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HBNKNWZC) works through this with prompts rather than answers, because the answers are not the sort anyone else can supply.

## Article: Meal paralysis: why you forget to eat, then cannot decide what to eat

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-meal-paralysis-forgetting-to-eat/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Standing in front of a full fridge, hungry, unable to pick anything. Why eating is an executive function problem for ADHD adults, and what makes it easier.

The fridge is full. You are hungry, genuinely hungry, the kind that has started to make you irritable. You open the door, look at everything in it, close the door, and eat a handful of dry cereal standing up.

It is one of the stranger experiences to try explaining to someone who has not had it, because every element of the problem is apparently solved. There is food. You can cook. You want to eat. And none of that is enough.

### Key takeaways

- Eating is a multi-step executive task, which is where it breaks, rather than at wanting food.
- ADHD often blunts hunger signals until hunger arrives as an emergency.
- Deciding costs more than cooking does, so removing the decision helps most.
- A short rotation of repeated meals beats variety, and the guilt about that is misplaced.
- Food that requires nothing, available at all times, prevents the worst days.

### Why eating is harder than it looks

Making a meal is not one task. It is a sequence: notice you are hungry, decide what to have, check you have the components, choose a recipe, prepare, cook, serve, eat, clear up. Nine steps, several of which require decisions, with a delay between effort and reward.

That is a demanding chain for an ADHD brain even on a good day. On a bad day the chain breaks at step two and you eat cereal.

The hunger signal itself is often unreliable. Many people with ADHD describe interoception that runs quiet: you do not notice hunger building gradually, so there is no gentle prompt at the point where cooking would still be easy. Instead hunger arrives suddenly and at full volume, usually at the moment your capacity to do anything about it is lowest. Hungry is also the state in which decision-making is worst, which makes the whole thing self-defeating.

Stimulant medication can suppress appetite further, which is worth knowing and worth raising with a prescriber if you are losing weight or regularly eating nothing until evening.

Then there is the delay problem. Cooking is forty minutes of effort for a reward that arrives at the end. Something immediate and processed is thirty seconds for a reward now. For a brain that discounts delayed rewards steeply, that comparison is not close, and this has nothing to do with knowing which option is better.

### The decision is the expensive part

Most people assume the hard part is the cooking. In my experience the decision costs more.

Deciding what to eat is an open-ended choice with too many options, no clear criteria, and a mild penalty for getting it wrong. That is precisely the shape of problem that produces paralysis. Combine it with hunger, which has already degraded your decision-making, and you get the fridge scene.

This is why meal planning advice so often fails us. It asks you to make seven of these decisions at once, on a Sunday, which is more of the expensive thing rather than less. The people for whom meal planning works are generally people who did not find the decision hard in the first place.

> The fix is not better decisions about food. It is fewer decisions about food.

### What actually helps

Shrink the menu, hard. Pick four or five meals you can make nearly automatically and rotate them. Not for a week. Indefinitely. The variety you lose is worth less than the decisions you stop having to make, and the meals become cheap to execute because you stop needing to think about any of the steps.

People feel guilty about this. The guilt comes from a cultural idea that eating should be varied and interesting, which is a fine aspiration for people who are eating at all. Eating the same four dinners reliably is a substantially better outcome than cooking something interesting twice a week and having cereal the other five nights.

Keep food that requires nothing. Not as a nutritional strategy, as a floor. Things that can be eaten with no preparation, no decision, and no washing up, kept somewhere visible. On the worst days this is the difference between eating badly and not eating, and not eating makes everything else worse, including the capacity to make a better choice later.

Eat on a schedule rather than on hunger, if your hunger signal is unreliable. An alarm is a cruder instrument than appetite and considerably more dependable. Eating something small at a fixed time prevents the emergency-hunger state in which no good decision is available.

Use the convenience options deliberately instead of guiltily. Pre-chopped vegetables, frozen everything, the meal kit, the supermarket delivery. These remove steps from the chain, and steps are the actual problem. Paying slightly more to remove three steps from a nine-step process is a reasonable trade, not a moral failure.

And separate cooking from clearing up. The prospect of the washing up stops a lot of meals from happening. One pan, or a plate you accept will sit there until tomorrow, removes a blocker that has nothing to do with food.

### The shame part

There is usually a layer of embarrassment about this that makes it harder to address.

Feeding yourself is treated as the most basic form of adult competence. Being unable to do it reliably, while being perfectly capable of complex work, feels absurd, and it is the kind of thing people hide. I have met very few people who talk about this openly, and a great many who recognise it instantly when someone else does.

It helps to see it accurately. This is an executive function problem that happens to involve food. It is not a character failure, and it does not respond to being more disciplined about it, which is the approach most of us have already tried for years.

### When it is more than this

Worth saying plainly: if your eating is restricted by texture, colour, smell or a fear of particular foods to the point where it affects your health, that may be ARFID or another eating disorder rather than executive dysfunction, and those overlap with both autism and ADHD at higher rates.

Same if you are regularly not eating for long stretches, losing weight unintentionally, or the distress around food is significant. That is a conversation with a doctor. The strategies here are for a logistics problem, and they are the wrong tool for a clinical one.

### Common questions

### Why do I forget to eat all day and then binge at night?

Because unmet hunger does not disappear, it accumulates, and the evening is usually when demands finally drop and the signal breaks through. By then you are extremely hungry and your capacity to make considered choices is at its lowest. Eating something at fixed times during the day, whether or not you feel like it, is what most reliably interrupts this.

### Is forgetting to eat an ADHD symptom?

It is not a diagnostic criterion, and it is a very commonly reported experience among ADHD adults. It is usually attributed to a combination of reduced interoception, absorption in tasks, and appetite suppression from stimulant medication where that applies.

### Is it bad to eat the same meals every day?

Nutritionally it is worth having some variety across your rotation, and a doctor or dietitian can advise properly on that. Practically, a short rotation you actually eat beats a varied plan you abandon. If you want reassurance about the specifics of what you are eating, that is a good question for a professional rather than a reason to go back to deciding nightly.

### Does medication make this worse?

Stimulant medication commonly reduces appetite, which can make the forgetting worse even as it helps elsewhere. It is worth tracking and raising with your prescriber, particularly if you are losing weight or finding you eat nothing until the evening. Do not adjust medication on your own.

### What is the single most useful change?

Pick four meals and stop choosing. Almost everything else is downstream of removing the decision. [The ADHD Eating Reset](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GDH6R4DL) builds out the rotation and the no-preparation floor in more detail.

## Article: The 2 a.m. spiral: why ADHD overthinking happens at night

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-overthinking-2am-spiral/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Replaying a conversation from 2014 at two in the morning. Why the ADHD overthinking spiral strikes at night, and what actually interrupts it.

It is almost always something small. A phrase you used in a meeting. The way you said goodbye to someone at a party in 2014. A message you sent that got a short reply.

During the day these would not survive five seconds of attention. At two in the morning they are the most important thing that has ever happened, and you will examine them from every angle for an hour, reaching no conclusion, with work in six hours.

### Key takeaways

- The spiral arrives at night because the distractions that were suppressing it are gone.
- It is rumination, which feels like problem-solving but produces no decisions.
- Arguing with the content extends it, because engaging is what keeps it running.
- Interrupting it needs enough cognitive load to occupy the loop, rather than relaxation.
- Phone use in bed reliably makes it worse, and it is also the hardest thing to change.

### Why night

Nothing about the thoughts is nocturnal. What changes is everything else.

All day your attention has been occupied. Work, noise, conversation, music, screens. For an ADHD brain that is understimulated by default, this is a continuous supply of input, and it keeps the loop suppressed by crowding it out.

Then you lie down in a dark, quiet room with no input at all. The understimulation becomes acute, and your brain goes looking for something to process. What it finds is the unresolved material: the social interaction with an ambiguous outcome, the thing you said that might have landed badly, the task you have not started.

Ambiguous social information is the preferred fuel, because it cannot be resolved. A problem with an answer gets solved and released. A question like did that person find me annoying has no available answer, so it can be worked indefinitely, which is exactly what makes it so sticky.

Tiredness makes it worse rather than better. The inhibition that would normally let you drop a thought is at its weakest when you are exhausted, which is why the same thought you dismissed at eleven is immovable at two.

### It feels productive, which is the trap

The spiral presents itself as working on something. You are analysing, considering, examining the evidence. It has the texture of problem-solving.

The difference is that problem-solving terminates. It produces a decision, an action, or a conclusion that you can act on tomorrow. Rumination produces another lap. If you have gone round the same material four times and arrived nowhere, that is not analysis, whatever it feels like.

This matters because it tells you which tool to use. You do not need to think harder about the thing. You need to stop the mechanism, which is a different task entirely.

> If you have examined it four times and reached nothing, a fifth pass is not going to be the one.

### Why reasoning with it fails

The intuitive response is to answer the thought. Work out whether you really did say something awkward, decide it was fine, and move on.

This almost never works, for two reasons.

The first is that resolving one item does not close the loop. It just frees capacity for the next item, and there is always a next item. Fourteen years of social interactions is a deep archive. You cannot clear it by adjudicating entries one at a time.

The second is that engaging is what sustains it. The loop needs something to process, and your attention is the thing it is processing with. Arguing with the content is feeding it.

Trying to force the thoughts out is similarly counterproductive. Suppression requires monitoring whether the thought is present, which means holding it in mind, which is the thing you were trying to stop.

### What actually interrupts it

The approach that works is giving the loop something else to chew on, at the right difficulty.

It has to be demanding enough to occupy you. Relaxation usually fails, because a calm, low-input activity leaves exactly the kind of spare capacity the spiral is using. What works better is something that requires mild, continuous cognitive effort: an audiobook or podcast you have to follow, counting backwards in sevens, naming things in a category, describing a familiar route in detail. Boring enough for sleep, occupying enough to displace the loop.

Writing it down works better than it sounds. Not journaling, and not analysing. Three lines, on paper, by the bed. Something like: worried I was short with Dan, will check tomorrow. The effect is that the thought stops having to be held, because holding it is partly about not wanting to lose it.

Getting up helps when twenty minutes have passed with no progress. Lying in the dark reinforces the association between bed and spiralling. Sit somewhere else, do something dull and dimly lit, go back when you feel sleepy. This is slow to pay off and it does pay off.

A deliberate worry slot during the day sounds artificial and works for a lot of people. Fifteen minutes, same time, where you address the things that keep surfacing. It gives the loop a legitimate appointment, which makes a surprising difference to how insistent it is at night.

And the physical things matter more than they should. Cold room, consistent timing, less caffeine later than you think is reasonable. None of this is exciting advice, and it moves the baseline.

### The phone

Worth addressing on its own, because it is the most common accelerant and the hardest to give up.

Phones at night do two incompatible things. They do occupy the loop, which is why reaching for one feels like relief. They also supply an endless stream of new, mildly activating material, which keeps you awake and frequently adds fresh items for the spiral to work with.

The other pattern here is revenge bedtime procrastination: staying up because the evening is the only part of the day that belongs to you, and going to sleep means it ends and tomorrow starts. That is not a sleep hygiene problem. It is usually a sign that there is not enough unclaimed time in your day, and the fix is upstream of bedtime.

If removing the phone entirely is not realistic, charging it across the room is the version most people can actually sustain. The requirement to stand up introduces enough friction to break the automatic reach.

### Common questions

### Why does overthinking get worse at night with ADHD?

Mostly because the external stimulation that was suppressing it disappears when you lie down. An understimulated brain in a dark, silent room generates its own input, and unresolved social material is the most available source. Reduced inhibition when tired makes the thoughts harder to drop than they were earlier in the day.

### Is this anxiety or ADHD?

They overlap heavily and frequently coexist. Rumination is strongly associated with anxiety, and ADHD contributes understimulation, poor inhibition and a large stock of unresolved social moments. If the worry is persistent, occurs across most areas of your life, or is affecting your functioning during the day, that is worth discussing with a professional rather than attributing to ADHD and managing alone.

### Does melatonin or medication help?

That is a question for a prescriber, and the answer depends on your situation. What I can say is that sleep timing is genuinely different for many ADHD adults, and it is a reasonable thing to raise at an appointment rather than something to solve purely with willpower and routine.

### Why do I remember embarrassing things from years ago?

Because they were never resolved, and unresolved social information is the most reliable fuel for this. Memories with a strong emotional charge and no conclusion stay available, and the quiet of the night is when your brain goes looking for something to process.

### What should I try first?

An audiobook on a sleep timer, and three lines on paper by the bed. The combination displaces the loop and removes the need to keep holding things in mind. [The ADHD Overthinking Reset](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GDGK3RLK) goes into the interrupt techniques in more depth.

## Article: Decision paralysis: why small choices cost the most

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-decision-paralysis/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Why an ADHD brain can make a big decision quickly, then lose forty minutes choosing a bin bag. How analysis paralysis works and what gets you unstuck.

I have changed career on a fortnight's reflection and lost most of an evening to choosing between two almost identical kettles.

That ratio is the thing worth explaining, because it looks like inconsistency and it is not. The small decisions are harder, and there is a reason for it.

### Key takeaways

- Small decisions are often harder than large ones, because nothing forces them to close.
- Without a clear criterion, every option looks equally defensible and comparison never ends.
- Paralysis is frequently emotional avoidance rather than genuine uncertainty.
- Setting a stopping rule in advance works better than trying to decide faster.
- Most small decisions are reversible, and treating them as reversible removes most of the weight.

### Why small decisions are harder

Big decisions arrive with structure. They have deadlines, consequences that focus the mind, and usually other people involved who need an answer. The structure forces a conclusion.

Small decisions have none of that. Nobody needs your kettle decision by Thursday. There is no penalty for taking another hour. So the process has no natural end, and without an end it can continue indefinitely.

Worse, the options in small decisions tend to be close together. Two kettles that do the same thing differ in ways that are real but tiny, which means the comparison can always be refined further. There is always another review, another specification, another dimension you have not weighed. The closer the options, the longer you can legitimately keep comparing, which is the opposite of how it should work.

Then there is the missing criterion. For a big decision you usually know what matters. For small ones you often do not, so you end up trying to optimise across everything at once: price, quality, reviews, appearance, longevity, delivery time, ethics of the manufacturer. No option wins on all of them, so no option ever clearly wins.

> Two near-identical options cannot be meaningfully separated, which is exactly why you can keep trying forever.

### When it is avoidance wearing a disguise

Sometimes the paralysis is not about the decision at all.

If choosing means committing, and committing means possibly being wrong, then not choosing keeps every outcome theoretically still available. Deliberating feels productive while actually functioning as a way of staying still.

The signs are fairly reliable once you know them. Researching long past the point where new information is changing anything. Reaching a conclusion and then reopening it. Feeling relief when something prevents the decision from having to be made. Asking several people and discounting whichever answer you did not want.

Rejection sensitivity sharpens this considerably. If being wrong feels catastrophic rather than inconvenient, deferring the decision is doing emotional work, and no amount of additional information will resolve something that is not an information problem.

### What actually helps

Decide how you will decide, before you start. One criterion, chosen in advance. Cheapest that meets a basic standard. Best reviewed under a price. The one available soonest. Having a rule converts an open comparison into a lookup, and a lookup terminates.

Put a time limit on it and treat the limit as binding. Ten minutes for anything under a certain value, and when the timer goes you take whatever is currently ahead. The quality of a decision made in ten minutes versus ninety is usually indistinguishable at this scale, and the eighty minutes are gone either way.

Cut the list to three. Most paralysis is caused by too many options, and the difficulty rises fast with the number. Take the first three that meet your criterion, discard everything else without examining it, and choose among those.

Check reversibility explicitly. Most small decisions are easily undone: returns, cancellations, trying again next week. Asking what happens if this is wrong usually produces an answer like I return it, which deflates most of the pressure. Keep the careful deliberation for decisions that are genuinely hard to reverse, which are rarer than they feel.

Automate repeating decisions permanently. Anything you decide more than once a month deserves a default: same lunch, same brand, same supermarket slot. The decision is made once and never again. This is where the largest savings are, because recurring decisions are where most of the time actually goes.

And accept good enough as a target rather than a compromise. The pursuit of the best option is what most small decisions founder on, and the gap between the best choice and a decent one at this scale is almost always smaller than the cost of finding it.

### If you are stuck right now

Pick the one you were leaning toward in the first ten seconds.

That instinct is usually as good as anything that follows, and in my experience the extended deliberation after it rarely changes the answer. It mostly adds justification to a decision already made, or exhausts you into choosing nothing at all, which is the worst available outcome because you have paid the full cost and received none of the benefit.

If you genuinely have no instinct, the options are close enough that it does not matter. Take either. The symmetry that makes the choice hard is the same symmetry that makes it low stakes.

### Common questions

### Why can I make big decisions easily but not small ones?

Big decisions come with deadlines, consequences and other people, all of which force closure. Small ones have no structure, close options, and no obvious criterion, so the comparison can continue indefinitely. The size of the decision and the difficulty of making it are not well correlated.

### Is decision paralysis an ADHD thing?

Difficulty with decision-making is commonly reported by ADHD adults and relates to executive function: holding options in mind, weighing future outcomes, and inhibiting further deliberation. It is not exclusive to ADHD, and it is also strongly associated with anxiety, which frequently coexists.

### How do I stop researching?

Decide the stopping condition before you begin, because you will not be able to judge it reliably once you are inside the process. Three options, ten minutes, one criterion. The point is that the limit is set by a version of you who is not currently in the loop.

### Does this get worse when I am tired?

Usually, and noticeably. Decision-making degrades with fatigue, and inhibition degrades with it, so you are both less able to choose and less able to stop deliberating. Postponing non-urgent decisions when you are depleted is a reasonable strategy rather than an avoidance.

### What is the single most useful habit?

Defaults for anything recurring. Deciding once and never again removes the largest share of decisions from your week, and it is where the biggest return is. [The ADHD Decision Reset](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GDMWFDZ7) covers building those defaults and the stopping rules in more depth.

## Article: Rejection sensitive dysphoria: when criticism feels physical

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/rejection-sensitive-dysphoria/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Rejection sensitive dysphoria makes criticism feel physical. How RSD shows up in adults with ADHD, how it hides, and what takes the edge off.

Your manager sends a message that says "Can we chat tomorrow?" with no further detail. By the time you finish reading it, your chest is tight, your face is hot, and you have already drafted your resignation in your head.

Tomorrow's chat turns out to be about holiday dates.

If that pattern is familiar, the term you may be looking for is rejection sensitive dysphoria. It is not a formal diagnosis and you will not find it in a diagnostic manual, but it is widely used in ADHD communities because it names something a great many of us recognise on first hearing.

### Key takeaways

- RSD is intense emotional pain in response to real or perceived rejection, criticism or failure.
- The reaction arrives fast, feels physical, and is wildly out of proportion to the trigger.
- It often hides behind people-pleasing, perfectionism, or avoiding anything you might fail at.
- The feeling cannot be argued away in the moment, but the response to it can be delayed.
- It is common in ADHD and overlaps with anxiety, so persistent distress is worth taking to a professional.

### What it feels like

The defining feature is speed. There is no gradual build. One moment you are fine, the next you are flooded, and the flood is physical: heat in the face, a drop in the stomach, sometimes tears that arrive before you have decided anything.

The second feature is scale. A minor piece of feedback lands with the weight of a verdict on your whole person. The distance between "this paragraph could be tighter" and "you are fundamentally not good enough" collapses to nothing.

The third is that it does not need actual rejection. Ambiguity is enough. A delayed reply, a flat tone, someone leaving a meeting early, a friend who seems slightly quieter than usual. The brain fills the gap with the worst available interpretation and then responds to that interpretation as fact.

People describe it as a burn, or a punch, or the floor going. Those are not exaggerations. The response is out of proportion to the trigger, but the pain itself is real.

### How it hides

RSD does not always look like an emotional reaction from outside. Often it looks like a personality.

People-pleasing is one of the most common disguises. If disapproval hurts that much, preventing it becomes a full-time job: saying yes to everything, never disagreeing, reading every room for signs of displeasure, apologising pre-emptively.

Perfectionism is another. Work gets polished far past the point of usefulness because handing it in means exposing it to judgement. Or it never gets handed in at all.

Avoidance is the quietest one. Not applying for the job. Not sending the message. Not starting the project, the relationship, the hobby, because trying means the possibility of failing, and failing means the burn. From outside this reads as a lack of ambition. From inside it is a reasonable calculation by someone who knows exactly how much it will hurt.

And sometimes it looks like anger. The pain turns outward, fast, at whoever triggered it. That tends to damage the relationships the sensitivity was trying to protect, which then feeds more fear of rejection.

> From outside, RSD often looks like a personality: the people-pleaser, the perfectionist, the person who never quite tries.

### Why ADHD and RSD go together

The honest answer is that the mechanism is not fully understood, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. What is well described is that emotional dysregulation, difficulty managing the intensity of emotions, is extremely common in adults with ADHD, even though it is not part of the formal diagnostic criteria. RSD reads like a specific, sharp form of that.

There is also a history argument that many people find persuasive from their own lives. If you grew up with undiagnosed ADHD, you probably received a great deal of correction. Forgotten homework, lost belongings, "you're not applying yourself", "why can't you just". Years of that can build a very sensitive alarm around criticism, because criticism was frequent and often aimed at things you could not control.

Autistic adults describe similar patterns, often tangled up with masking. When you have spent years monitoring other people's faces for signs that your performance is slipping, any sign of disapproval carries extra charge.

### What helps

The feeling itself does not respond well to logic in the moment. Telling yourself it is an overreaction while you are mid-flood is about as effective as telling yourself a burn does not hurt. What you can change is what you do while the feeling is running.

Name it, specifically. "This is RSD" is more useful than "I'm upset", because it labels the reaction as a known pattern rather than accurate information about the situation. It does not stop the pain. It does stop you treating the pain as evidence.

Put a delay between the feeling and any response. No replies, no decisions, no resignation emails for a fixed period. An hour is often enough. The flood usually passes faster than it feels like it will, and almost every regrettable action happens inside it.

Check the story against the facts once the intensity has dropped. Write down what actually happened, in neutral language, and then write down the story your brain built on top of it. "Manager asked to chat tomorrow" and "I am about to be fired" are very different sentences, and seeing them side by side is often enough.

Ask, if it is safe to. "Is everything okay between us?" or "Was there something specific about this you'd like changed?" feels terrifying and usually produces a mundane answer. Many people with RSD have spent years avoiding questions that would have resolved the uncertainty in a sentence.

Choose your exposures. Some environments run on constant feedback, public evaluation and ambiguous signals. If you have a choice, it is reasonable to factor RSD into it, the same way you would factor in any other known sensitivity.

And tell one or two trusted people. Partners and close friends who know about RSD can be more explicit: "I'm not annoyed, just tired" removes an enormous amount of guesswork.

### When to get help

If the reactions are frequent, severe, or are pushing you away from work and relationships you care about, it is worth raising with a professional. RSD overlaps heavily with anxiety and depression, and those deserve proper assessment rather than self-management alone. Some people with ADHD find that treatment changes their emotional reactivity, and that is a conversation to have with a prescriber.

If criticism or rejection ever leaves you thinking about harming yourself, please contact a crisis line or emergency services where you are.

### Common questions

### Is rejection sensitive dysphoria a real diagnosis?

No. It is not a formal diagnosis and does not appear in diagnostic manuals. It is a widely used description, particularly in ADHD communities, for an intense emotional response to perceived rejection or criticism. The experience is real even though the label is informal.

### Is RSD only an ADHD thing?

It is most often discussed in relation to ADHD, but similar patterns are described by autistic people and by people with anxiety and other conditions. Sensitivity to rejection is a human trait. What people with RSD describe is the speed and intensity of the response, which goes well beyond the ordinary.

### How is RSD different from just being sensitive?

Mainly in speed, scale and physicality. People with RSD describe an almost instant, overwhelming reaction to minor or ambiguous signals, felt in the body, that can take hours to settle. Ordinary sensitivity tends to be proportionate and to fade quickly.

### Can RSD be treated?

Some people find that ADHD treatment reduces their emotional reactivity, and therapy can help with the patterns built around it, such as avoidance and people-pleasing. Those are conversations for a doctor or therapist. The practical strategies here help with managing reactions, not with treating anything.

### What can I do in the moment?

Label it as RSD, then delay any response for at least an hour. The feeling will be loud, but most of the damage comes from acting inside it. [The ADHD Overthinking Reset](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-overthinking-reset/) has a section on RSD spirals specifically.

## Article: Body doubling: why ADHD tasks get easier when someone else is in the room

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-body-doubling/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Body doubling means working with someone present who is not helping. Why it helps ADHD adults start tasks, and how to set it up.

For years I could not do my tax paperwork. I could do it, technically. I understood every form. I just could not start, and it sat on the desk for weeks, getting heavier.

Then someone sat on the other end of the sofa reading a book, and I finished the whole lot in an afternoon. They did not help. They did not even look at it. They were just there.

That is body doubling, and it sounds far too simple to work. For a lot of ADHD adults it is the single most reliable way of getting started on anything.

### Key takeaways

- Body doubling is doing a task while another person is present, without them helping.
- It works for starting and continuing tasks, especially boring or avoided ones.
- The other person can be in the room, on a video call, or a stranger on a co-working stream.
- Matching the format to the task matters more than finding the perfect partner.
- It is a legitimate tool, not a crutch, and needing it says nothing about your competence.

### What it actually is

The definition is short. You do your task. Another person is present while you do it. They are not supervising, teaching or helping. Usually they are doing their own thing.

It can be a partner on the sofa, a friend at the kitchen table, a colleague in a quiet room, a video call where both of you work silently with cameras on, or a recorded video of someone studying. Some people go to a café for the same reason, and get the effect from strangers.

People with ADHD often discover it by accident and then feel slightly embarrassed about it, as though needing an audience to do the washing up is something to hide. It is not. It is a tool that suits a particular brain, the same way glasses suit particular eyes.

### Why it works

I want to be careful here, because the honest answer is that nobody has a complete explanation, and plenty of confident ones circulate online. What I can describe is what people with ADHD consistently report.

The presence of another person seems to anchor attention. Alone, the mind drifts, and there is nothing pulling it back. With someone there, there is a gentle external reference point. You notice when you have wandered off, because you are briefly aware of being seen doing nothing.

There is a mild accountability effect, even when the other person is not paying attention. Saying "I'm going to do my emails now" out loud to someone makes it slightly more real than deciding it in your head.

It also makes the task feel less lonely. A lot of avoided tasks are avoided partly because they are isolating and grim. Another person nearby changes the emotional temperature, and the task becomes something you are doing in company rather than alone in a room with a pile.

And it breaks the starting problem. The hardest moment in most ADHD tasks is the transition from not doing it to doing it. A body double turns that into an appointment: we start at two.

### Ways to do it

In person is the strongest version for most people. Agree a time, sit in the same space, each work on your own thing. A few words at the start about what you are each doing helps. Then stop talking.

Virtual body doubling works surprisingly well. A video call with a friend, both muted, both working. Cameras on seems to matter for many people, even though nobody is watching.

Structured co-working sessions are useful when you do not have a willing friend. There are services and community sessions built around this, where strangers join timed blocks, state a goal at the start, and report back at the end. The structure adds an extra layer of commitment.

Recorded videos of people working are the lightest version. They help some people a lot and others not at all. They are free and available at three in the morning, which counts for something.

Even a phone call can work. Some people ring a friend, put the phone on speaker, and both clean their kitchens.

### Making it work

Match the format to the task. Admin and paperwork often need a quiet, focused double. Physical tasks like cleaning work well with a chatty one, or with someone on a call doing the same chore.

Say the task out loud at the start. Specifically. "I'm going to open the three letters from the bank" works better than "I'm going to do admin". Reporting back at the end, even briefly, closes the loop.

Keep the talking to a minimum during focused tasks. Body doubling turns into socialising very easily, which is pleasant and produces nothing.

Schedule it. The value is partly in the appointment. "We'll do it some time" has the same problem as every other ADHD intention.

Reciprocate if you can. Being someone else's body double costs very little and makes it easier to ask again.

### When it does not suit you

For some autistic people, and some AuDHD people, the presence of another person is draining rather than anchoring. Monitoring someone else, even passively, uses up exactly the capacity the task needed. If body doubling leaves you more tired than the task would have, try the lightest version, a silent video or a recorded stream, or skip it.

It can also become a dependency if it is the only way you can start anything. That is not a disaster, but it is worth keeping a few other starting tools alongside it, for the days when nobody is available.

### Common questions

### Is body doubling a real ADHD strategy?

It is a widely used and widely recommended strategy among people with ADHD and the coaches who work with them. The research base is still small, so it is better described as a well-established practical tool than as a proven treatment. Plenty of people find it works when other things have not.

### Does the other person have to be doing the same task?

No. Usually they are doing something completely different. The point is their presence, not their help. Some people find a double working on a similar task slightly more motivating, but it is not necessary.

### Does virtual body doubling work as well as in person?

For many people it works well, though in-person tends to be stronger. Cameras on and a brief statement of goals at the start seem to help a virtual session a lot.
