### Why can I only clean when someone is coming over?

That is closely related. An approaching visitor creates urgency and a sense of being seen, which are two of the things a body double provides. Booking a body doubling session can recreate some of that without needing the guest.

### What if I have no one to ask?

Use structured co-working sessions with strangers or recorded study-with-me videos. Both are free or cheap and available at any hour. [The Late-Diagnosed ADHD Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/late-diagnosed-adhd-workbook/) covers starting tasks and the wall between knowing and doing in more depth.

## Article: Time blindness: why ADHD makes you late, and what actually helps

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-time-blindness/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Time blindness makes ADHD adults late despite caring. Why time splits into now and not now, and how to move time out of your head.

You know the meeting is at ten. You know it takes twenty minutes to get there. At 9:52 you are still in the shower, and you could not tell anyone how it got to be 9:52.

People who are reliably on time tend to assume lateness means not caring. For a lot of ADHD adults it is closer to the opposite: you cared enough to think about the meeting all morning, and still had no felt sense of the morning passing.

The usual name for this is time blindness. It is a community term rather than a clinical one, and it describes the experience well.

### Key takeaways

- Time blindness is difficulty feeling time pass and estimating how long things take.
- ADHD time tends to split into "now" and "not now", with very little in between.
- It is a perception problem, so effort and caring do not fix it.
- The solution is to make time visible and external, rather than trying to feel it better.
- Estimates can be calibrated, but only by measuring, never by guessing harder.

### Now and not now

The most useful description I have come across is that ADHD time has two settings. There is now, which is vivid and urgent. And there is not now, which covers everything else, from an hour away to next year, and all of it feels roughly the same distance off.

That explains a lot of otherwise baffling behaviour. A deadline in three weeks does not register as more urgent than one in three months, because both are not now. Then it becomes now, suddenly, and everything happens in a panic.

It also explains the shower at 9:52. Ten o'clock was not now while you were getting ready. It was a fact you knew, not a pressure you felt. The pressure only arrives when the time has already gone.

### Estimates that are always wrong

The second part is estimation, and it fails in a consistent direction.

Most people with ADHD underestimate how long things take, often by a lot. Not because of optimism exactly, but because the estimate is built from the core of the task and leaves out everything around it. Getting to the shop takes ten minutes, in the sense that the drive takes ten minutes. It does not include finding keys, finding the other shoe, going back for the bag, the queue at the junction.

Transitions are where most of the time goes and where the estimate has nothing. Stopping one thing, getting up, moving, starting another. Each feels instant and each takes several minutes.

And hyperfocus breaks estimation completely. An hour of absorbed work and five minutes of absorbed work can feel identical from the inside.

> You cannot feel your way to better time sense. You have to move time outside your head, where you can see it.

### Waiting mode

A related pattern that many people only recognise once it is named: waiting mode.

You have an appointment at three. It is ten in the morning. And the whole day is now gone, because you cannot settle into anything. Starting a task feels risky, since you might lose track of time and miss the appointment, so you hover, half-doing small things, until three o'clock finally arrives.

It is time blindness turned into anxiety. You know you cannot trust your sense of time, so your brain refuses to let you do anything absorbing. The result is a day spent producing nothing while technically free.

Alarms help here more than anything else, specifically because they let your brain stop guarding the time.

### What actually helps

Everything that works follows the same principle: take time out of your head and put it somewhere you can see or hear it.

Visible clocks, everywhere. In every room you use, including the bathroom. Many people find analogue clocks easier than digital, because the shape of time remaining is visible rather than calculated. A visual timer that shows a shrinking coloured segment is the same idea in a more focused form.

Alarms for leaving, not for the event. An alarm at ten for a ten o'clock meeting is useless. Work backwards: meeting at ten, twenty minutes to get there, ten minutes to get out of the door, so the alarm is at 9:30, with a warning at 9:20. Set them as fixed habits rather than one-off reminders.

Pad every estimate by a fixed multiplier. Take your gut estimate and multiply it. Many people use 1.5 or 2. It feels absurd and it will still occasionally be wrong in the other direction, but it is much closer than the raw guess.

Calibrate with real measurement. For one week, time a handful of recurring tasks: getting ready, the commute, a load of washing, the weekly shop. Write the real numbers down. Real data beats intuition every time, and it is the only thing that actually improves your estimates.

Put everything in a calendar, including things that do not feel like appointments. Travel time. Getting-ready time. Lunch. If it is not in the calendar, it does not exist in your sense of time.

Use timers inside tasks. A timer every twenty or thirty minutes during absorbed work gives you a regular check-in with reality, and it works against hyperfocus quietly eating an afternoon.

And for waiting mode, set the alarm, trust the alarm, and deliberately start something absorbing. The alarm is doing the time-keeping job so your brain does not have to.

### Telling other people

Time blindness is very easy to read as disrespect, and it costs relationships. A short honest explanation tends to help more than repeated apologies, especially paired with visible effort: "I'm terrible with time, so I've set three alarms for this." People are generally more forgiving of a known difficulty being managed than of what looks like carelessness.

### Common questions

### Is time blindness an official ADHD symptom?

The term is informal and does not appear in diagnostic criteria. Difficulty with time management and with estimating time is very commonly reported by people with ADHD, and it relates to the executive functions involved in planning and organising.

### Why am I always late even when I try hard?

Because effort does not fix a perception problem. If you cannot feel time passing accurately, trying harder to feel it does not help. External tools such as visible clocks, leaving alarms and padded estimates work because they replace the perception you do not have.

### What is ADHD waiting mode?

It is when an upcoming appointment prevents you from doing anything else beforehand, because you do not trust yourself to keep track of time. Hours can disappear this way. Setting reliable alarms so your brain can stop guarding the time is the most common fix.

### Do analogue clocks really help?

Many people with ADHD find them easier, because the remaining time is visible as space on the clock face rather than as a number you have to subtract. It is a cheap thing to try. Visual countdown timers work on the same principle.

### What should I try first?

Leaving alarms, set backwards from the time you need to walk out the door. That single change prevents more lateness than anything else. [The Late-Diagnosed ADHD Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/late-diagnosed-adhd-workbook/) covers time blindness as part of its section on executive function.

## Article: ADHD task paralysis: when you cannot start, even though you want to

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-task-paralysis/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: ADHD paralysis is knowing exactly what to do and being unable to begin. Why it happens, why it is not laziness, and how to get over the wall.

There is a particular kind of afternoon that people without ADHD do not seem to have. You know what you need to do. You want to do it. It is not difficult. You have the time. And you sit there for three hours, not doing it, and not doing anything else either.

That is not rest. It is not procrastination in the ordinary sense, because you are not off enjoying something else. It is a sort of frozen idling, with a growing sense of dread, and at the end of it you have neither done the task nor had a break.

People call this task paralysis, or ADHD paralysis. It is one of the most common and least understood parts of adult ADHD.

### Key takeaways

- Task paralysis is being unable to start a task you want and intend to do.
- It comes from executive dysfunction, mostly the part of the brain's machinery that handles starting.
- Ambiguous, boring, large or emotionally loaded tasks trigger it most.
- Shrinking the first step until it is almost silly is the most reliable way in.
- Shame makes it worse, so treating it as a character flaw keeps you stuck.

### Why starting is the hard part

Most of the effort people with ADHD struggle with is not in doing a task. It is in starting it.

Initiation is one of the executive functions, and it is one that ADHD affects heavily. For a typical brain, deciding to do something and beginning to do it are close together. For an ADHD brain there can be a gap between them that will not close, no matter how clearly you have decided.

Some tasks make the gap much wider.

Ambiguous ones, first. "Sort out the car insurance" has no obvious first move. Which website? Which document? What exactly counts as sorted? Every unclear step is a small decision, and a pile of small decisions is enough to freeze the whole thing.

Then boring ones. An ADHD brain runs heavily on interest, novelty and urgency. A dull task with no deadline provides none of them, so there is nothing to push you over the threshold.

Large ones too. When a task is big enough that you cannot see its end, the brain treats starting it as committing to all of it.

And emotionally loaded ones, which may be the biggest group. The tax return you have failed at before. The email to someone you have let down. Anything with a history of shame attached accumulates weight every time you avoid it.

> A common image in ADHD circles is a wall: each failed attempt adds another brick, until a five-minute task stands behind something enormous.

### It is not laziness

This is worth saying plainly, because most of us were told otherwise for years.

Laziness is not wanting to do something and choosing not to. Task paralysis is wanting to do something, choosing to do it, and finding that the choice does not convert into action. The two look identical from outside and feel nothing alike from inside.

The confusion does real damage. If you believe you are lazy, the obvious fix is to try harder, which means more pressure, more self-criticism, and more emotional weight on the task. Which makes the paralysis worse. The harder you push on the wall, the taller it gets.

### What helps

Every method that works does one of two things: it makes the first step smaller, or it adds something that pushes you across the gap.

Shrink the first step until it is almost silly. Not "do the tax return". Not even "find the tax documents". "Open the drawer where the tax documents might be." The first step should be so small that refusing it feels absurd. Once you have started, momentum often carries you further than you planned, and if it does not, you have still done one thing.

Define what done means before you begin. "Reply to the three most urgent emails" has an end. "Do my emails" does not. Tasks without a finish line are exhausting to start because they feel infinite.

Remove the decisions. If the task stalls on choices, make them in advance or make them arbitrary. Start with whichever email is at the top. Use the first form you find. Every decision you remove takes a brick out of the wall.

Borrow someone else's presence. Body doubling, having another person in the room or on a call while you work, is one of the most reliable ways through. Even a stranger on a co-working stream helps many people.

Set a timer for five minutes and give yourself permission to stop when it rings. Five minutes is tolerable for almost anything, and after five minutes the task is no longer unstarted.

Change something physical. Stand up, move to a different room, put on specific music, make a drink. A change of state can break the frozen loop when willpower cannot.

Add stimulation if the task is boring. Music, a podcast for mechanical tasks, doing it somewhere new, racing a timer. You are supplying the interest the task does not.

And when you are truly stuck, do a different useful task. If you cannot face the tax return, clearing the kitchen is still progress. Many people with ADHD get a great deal done this way, by productively avoiding the thing at the top of the list.

### When it is something else

Persistent inability to start anything at all, especially alongside low mood, loss of interest or exhaustion, can be a sign of burnout or depression rather than ordinary task paralysis. If the paralysis has spread to everything, or has lasted weeks, it is worth talking to a doctor.

### Common questions

### What is ADHD paralysis?

It is the experience of being unable to start a task despite wanting and intending to, often with a feeling of being frozen. It is linked to executive dysfunction, particularly difficulty with task initiation. The term is informal and widely used by people with ADHD.

### Is task paralysis the same as procrastination?

They overlap, but people usually mean something different. Procrastination often involves choosing something more appealing instead. Task paralysis frequently involves doing nothing at all, without enjoyment, while wanting to start. The experience is closer to being stuck than to avoiding.

### Why can I do hard things easily but not simple ones?

Hard things are often interesting, novel or urgent, which supplies the push an ADHD brain needs to start. Simple, boring tasks supply none of it. Difficulty and startability are barely related, which is one of the more confusing parts of ADHD.

### How do I get out of it right now?

Pick the smallest possible physical action connected to the task and do only that. Open the laptop. Pick up one item. Set a five-minute timer. Starting is the hard part, and making the start tiny is how you get across it.

### Does it get better?

The underlying difficulty with initiation tends to persist, but your toolkit improves, and so does your ability to spot paralysis early. [The ADHD Decision Reset](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-decision-reset/) has a section on task prioritisation for the specific version where every item on the list looks equally urgent.

## Article: Stimming and sensory overload in autistic adults

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/stimming-and-sensory-overload/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: How stimming helps autistic adults regulate, how sensory overload builds through the day, and the small changes that stop it tipping over.

If you are a late-identified autistic adult, there is a good chance someone told you to stop doing something as a child. Stop rocking. Sit still. Stop humming. Stop playing with your hands.

You probably stopped. Or rather, you moved it somewhere less visible: a foot tapping under the desk, a thumb rubbing a finger, chewing the inside of your cheek, clicking a pen. You kept doing it because it was doing a job. You just learned to hide it.

That job is regulation, and understanding it changes how the rest of sensory life makes sense.

### Key takeaways

- Stimming is repetitive movement or sound used to regulate, and it serves a purpose.
- Many autistic adults were trained to suppress it, often moving it somewhere hidden.
- Sensory overload builds gradually, then tips over quickly, and the build is the part to watch.
- Sensory needs differ by person, and many people both seek and avoid input in different senses.
- Small environmental changes usually give the fastest relief of anything available.

### What stimming is for

Stimming covers repetitive movements or sounds: rocking, hand-flapping, finger movements, tapping, humming, pacing, spinning objects, rubbing a texture. Everyone does a little of it. Autistic people tend to do more, and to rely on it more.

People describe it doing several things. It helps manage incoming sensory input, by providing a predictable sensation that competes with the unpredictable ones. It helps regulate emotion, whether that is calming down or expressing excitement. And it helps with focus, giving the body something to do so the mind can settle.

Seen that way, suppressing it is a bit like asking someone to stop blinking in a dusty room. You can do it for a while. It costs something the whole time.

### Unlearning the suppression

Many late-identified adults find that letting stimming back in is one of the most immediate improvements available after recognising they are autistic. It is also one of the more emotionally complicated ones, because it means undoing years of training that the movements were embarrassing.

It usually starts at home, alone. Rocking while watching television. Flapping when excited. Using a fidget object during calls with the camera off. People often describe a noticeable drop in background tension within days.

Out in public, it tends to be selective. Some stims are socially invisible and easy to use anywhere. Others people keep for safe spaces. That is a reasonable compromise, and there is no obligation to be visibly autistic at your own expense.

### How sensory overload builds

Sensory overload happens when the amount or intensity of sensory input exceeds what your brain can process. Noise, light, touch, smell, movement, temperature, and the effort of following conversation all add to the load.

The useful thing to understand is that it is cumulative. It does not arrive with the last sound. It arrives because of every sound since you woke up.

A typical day might go like this. The alarm is harsh. The shower is too hot. The commute is loud and crowded. The office has flickering lights and someone else's music. Lunch is in a busy canteen. None of these is unbearable alone. By four in the afternoon the total is enormous, and then a colleague's chair scrapes and you find yourself near tears or close to snapping, over a chair.

The chair was not the cause. It was the last unit on a load that had been building all day.

> The last sound before overload gets the blame. The whole day put you there.

### Warning signs

Most people have early signs they can learn to spot, usually well before the point of overload.

Irritability with no obvious cause is a common one. Sounds starting to feel sharper or more intrusive than usual. A tendency to stop following conversations. Wanting to pull your hood up or put headphones on. Clumsiness. An urge to leave a room without being able to say why. Stimming that becomes more intense or more frequent.

Interoception differences, difficulty sensing your own internal state, can make these harder to notice. Some people only realise they are overloaded once they are already there. Deliberately checking in at set times during the day helps when the internal signal is unreliable.

### Seeking and avoiding

Sensory profiles are not simply "too sensitive". Many people are over-sensitive in some senses and under-sensitive in others, or seek input in one sense to cope with too much in another.

You might find noise unbearable and crave deep pressure. You might hate bright light and love strong flavours. You might need to move constantly while being unable to tolerate light touch. Working out your own profile is far more useful than general advice.

A simple sensory audit helps. Go through each sense and note what you find hard, what you find soothing, and what you actively look for. Patterns appear quickly, and they point directly at what to change.

### What helps

Reduce input where you can, cheaply. Noise-reducing earplugs or noise-cancelling headphones, sunglasses or tinted lenses indoors, softer lighting at home, clothing chosen by how it feels. These are small changes that often make a large difference within days.

Plan exits. Knowing you can leave a loud place, and having a reason ready, lowers the load before you have even used it.

Build recovery into the day rather than waiting for the end. Ten minutes somewhere quiet at lunch can reset more of the load than an evening of trying to recover once it has all built up.

Create one low-input space at home. Dim, quiet, and not shared with anyone's noise. It does not have to be large. It has to be reliable.

Stim freely where it is safe. It is one of the most direct regulation tools you have.

And plan around big days honestly. A wedding, a conference, an office party will cost more than an ordinary day. Lighter days before and after are part of the event.

### Common questions

### Do adults stim?

Yes. Stimming does not stop in adulthood, although many adults, particularly those identified late, have learned to make it less visible. Common adult stims include tapping, leg bouncing, fidgeting with objects, humming, and rubbing fingers or fabric.

### Is stimming only an autistic thing?

No. Everyone stims to some degree, and people with ADHD often stim noticeably, particularly through fidgeting and movement. Autistic people tend to stim more and to rely on it more heavily for regulation.

### Is it bad to stim in public?

There is nothing wrong with stimming, and suppressing it has a real cost. Whether to stim visibly in public is a personal decision that depends on safety and context. Many people use less noticeable stims in public and freer ones in private.

### What does sensory overload feel like?

People describe a rising sense of pressure, irritability or panic, with sounds, lights or textures becoming painful or impossible to filter. Thinking and speaking can become difficult. If it continues to build, it can lead to a meltdown or shutdown.

### Where should I start?

With a sensory audit and one or two cheap changes, often earplugs and lighting. [The Late-Diagnosed Autistic Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/late-diagnosed-autistic-workbook/) has a full section on sensory life, including the audit and stimming without shame.

## Article: Autistic meltdown vs shutdown: what is happening, and what helps

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-meltdown-vs-shutdown/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Meltdowns and shutdowns are involuntary responses to overload, one outward and one inward. What each feels like, and what helps during one.

Adults are not supposed to have meltdowns. That is the message most autistic adults absorbed early, which is why a meltdown at forty tends to arrive with a second wave of shame on top of the first.

They happen anyway. So do shutdowns, which are quieter and much more often missed. Both are involuntary responses to overload, and understanding them takes a good deal of the shame out.

### Key takeaways

- A meltdown is an outward loss of control in response to overwhelm. A shutdown is an inward one.
- Neither is chosen, and neither is a tantrum aimed at getting something.
- Both usually result from accumulated load, so the final trigger is rarely the real cause.
- During either one, the most helpful thing is less: less input, fewer questions, more space.
- Learning your early warning signs is the most useful prevention there is.

### What a meltdown is

A meltdown happens when overwhelm exceeds the point where you can regulate your responses. Control of your reactions goes, temporarily.

It can look like crying that will not stop, shouting, intense agitation, pacing, hitting objects, or a need to escape immediately. Some people describe it from inside as a kind of storm, where they can sometimes observe what is happening and cannot stop it.

The comparison to a tantrum comes up constantly and is worth answering directly, because most people believe it. A tantrum is aimed at an outcome, and it often stops when the outcome is achieved or when there is no audience. A meltdown is not aimed at anything. Giving the person what they seem to want does not end it, and it happens just as much alone.

### What a shutdown is

A shutdown is the same overload turned inward. Instead of exploding, the system goes offline.

You become less responsive, sometimes almost unresponsive. Speech can become very difficult or stop altogether. Thinking slows. Movement becomes hard. You might sit or lie very still, staring, unable to answer simple questions or make the smallest decision.

Shutdowns are missed constantly, because they are quiet. From outside they can look like sulking, rudeness or being withdrawn. People get criticised for not replying or for "going silent", when what was happening was a system protecting itself from more input.

Many people, particularly those who learned early that outward reactions were unacceptable, have far more shutdowns than meltdowns.

> A meltdown is the system overflowing. A shutdown is the system switching itself off. Both are protection.

### What causes them

Usually not the thing that seems to cause them.

The visible trigger is often minor: a plan changing, a noise, a question at the wrong moment, a dropped glass. Underneath it is a load that has been accumulating for hours or days. Sensory input, social effort, masking, uncertainty, hunger, tiredness, changes in routine. Each one adds to the total. The trigger is just the moment the total crosses the line.

That is why the same event can be completely fine one day and the final straw the next. The event did not change. Your remaining capacity did.

Being in autistic burnout lowers the threshold considerably, so meltdowns and shutdowns often become more frequent during burnout, which can be frightening if you do not know why.

### Warning signs

Most people have signs before the line is crossed, even if they have learned to ignore them.

Common ones include rising irritability, sounds or lights becoming more intrusive, losing track of conversations, stimming becoming more intense, a strong urge to leave, clumsiness, difficulty finding words, and a sense of pressure building in the head or chest.

Interoception and alexithymia, difficulty sensing your internal state and naming emotions, can make these harder to catch. A practical way round it is to check in on a schedule rather than waiting to notice. "How loud does everything feel, out of ten?" at a few fixed times is cruder than intuition and more reliable.

### What helps during one

Less of everything. Fewer words, less light, less noise, fewer people.

If you are the one experiencing it, the priority is getting somewhere with less input, if you can. Headphones, a quiet room, a car, a bathroom. Leaving is allowed. Explaining can come later.

If you are supporting someone, do not ask lots of questions, do not try to reason with them, and do not touch them unless you know they want that. Say very little, calmly. Reduce the input around them. Make sure they are safe and stay nearby if that helps, at a distance if it does not. Wait.

For shutdowns in particular, do not demand answers. A shutdown often removes the ability to speak, and pressure to respond adds load.

### Afterwards

Recovery takes longer than the event. Exhaustion, a headache, emotional flatness or a need for a lot of sleep afterwards are common.

It is better not to dissect what happened straight away. Analysis is another demand, and you have nothing left. Once you have recovered, it can be useful to look back at what built up beforehand, not to assign blame, but to find the load you can reduce next time.

And try to drop the shame where you can. A meltdown or shutdown is a nervous system reaching its limit. It says something about the load, and nothing about your character.

### Getting support

If meltdowns or shutdowns are frequent, are getting worse, or involve any risk of harm to yourself or others, it is worth talking to a professional, ideally one who understands autistic adults. If you are ever in immediate danger, contact emergency services.

### Common questions

### What is the difference between a meltdown and a shutdown?

Both are involuntary responses to overwhelm. A meltdown is outward: crying, shouting, agitation or a need to escape. A shutdown is inward: withdrawing, going quiet, and sometimes losing the ability to speak or move easily. The same person can have both.

### Do autistic adults have meltdowns?

Yes. Meltdowns do not stop in adulthood, though many adults have learned to hold them in until they are alone, or experience shutdowns more often instead. Adult meltdowns are common and are frequently surrounded by a lot of shame.

### Is a meltdown the same as a tantrum?

No. A tantrum is aimed at an outcome and often stops when it is achieved or when there is no audience. A meltdown is an involuntary loss of control caused by overload. It is not aimed at anything, and it happens whether or not anyone is watching.

### How can I help someone having a meltdown?

Reduce the input around them, speak very little and calmly, avoid touching them unless you know they want it, and make sure they are safe. Do not try to reason with them or ask a series of questions. Give them time and space to come out of it.

### Can meltdowns be prevented?

Not always, but they can often be made less frequent by reducing the overall load and by learning your early warning signs. [The Late-Diagnosed Autistic Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/late-diagnosed-autistic-workbook/) covers reading your energy and sensory load before it reaches zero.

## Glossary

### ADHD

Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition that affects attention, impulse control, activity levels and the executive functions that organise behaviour. In adults it often shows up less as visible hyperactivity and more as difficulty starting tasks, managing time, regulating emotion and following through.

### The ADHD tax

A community term for the money, and sometimes time, lost to ADHD-related difficulties: late fees on bills you could afford, forgotten subscriptions, replacing things you already own, and paying extra for convenience when the cheaper option had too many steps. It is not an official financial or clinical term.

### Alexithymia

Difficulty identifying and describing your own emotions. It is a trait rather than a diagnosis, and it occurs more often in autistic people than in the general population. Someone with alexithymia may notice the physical side of a feeling, like a tight chest, without being able to name the emotion behind it.

### Analysis paralysis

Being unable to make a decision because you keep comparing options instead of choosing one. With ADHD it often hits small decisions hardest, because they have close options, no deadline and no obvious criterion, so the comparison never has to end.

### ARFID

Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, an eating disorder in which intake is limited by sensory sensitivity, fear of consequences such as choking, or low interest in food, rather than by concern about weight or body shape. It occurs at higher rates in autistic people and people with ADHD, and needs professional assessment rather than self-management.

### AuDHD

An informal term for someone who is both autistic and ADHD. It is not a separate diagnosis, since each condition is diagnosed on its own. The word exists because the combination produces conflicts, such as needing routine while craving novelty, that neither diagnosis describes alone.

### Autism

A lifelong neurodevelopmental difference affecting social communication, sensory processing, and a preference for predictability and focused interests. Clinically it is called autism spectrum disorder. Many autistic adults prefer the word autistic. Adults who mask are frequently identified late.

### Autistic burnout

A period of long-term exhaustion, loss of previously held skills, and reduced tolerance for sensory input, usually caused by sustained masking and demands that exceed capacity over months or years. It is widely described by autistic adults but is not a formal diagnosis. It differs from depression, although the two can occur together.

### Body doubling

Doing a task while another person is present, in the room or on a video call, without them helping. Many people with ADHD find it much easier to start and keep going this way, particularly with boring or avoided tasks.

### Double empathy problem

The idea that communication difficulties between autistic and non-autistic people run in both directions, rather than coming from an autistic deficit alone. Each group can find the other hard to read, and autistic people often communicate easily with one another.

### Echolalia

Repeating words or phrases heard elsewhere, either immediately or later. It is common in autism and can serve communication, processing or self-regulation. In adults it often takes the form of quotes or scripts borrowed from films, shows or other people.

### Emotional dysregulation

Difficulty managing the intensity and duration of emotional responses. It is not among the formal diagnostic criteria for ADHD, but it is very commonly reported by adults with ADHD and is a large part of how many of them experience the condition.

### Executive dysfunction

Difficulty with the executive functions: the mental processes used to plan, start, organise, switch between and finish tasks, hold information in mind, and manage time. It is central to ADHD and common in autism. It often feels like knowing exactly what to do and being unable to begin.

### Hyperfocus

Intense absorption in a task that is hard to break, often with lost awareness of time, hunger or tiredness. It is not under voluntary control: it attaches to whatever is interesting or urgent enough, which is not always the thing that needs doing.

### Interoception

The sense of your body's internal state, including hunger, thirst, temperature, needing the toilet, and the physical side of emotions. Differences in interoception are common in autism and ADHD, and they help explain forgetting to eat or only noticing overwhelm once it is already severe.

### Late diagnosis

Being identified as ADHD or autistic in adulthood rather than childhood. It is common among people who masked well, did well at school, or did not match the narrow descriptions used when they were young. It often brings relief and grief at the same time.

### Masking

Suppressing natural behaviour and performing expected behaviour to fit in: forcing eye contact, scripting conversations, hiding stimming, copying how other people act. It is common in autistic people and also occurs in ADHD. It is tiring to sustain and is strongly associated with burnout.

### Meal paralysis

Being hungry and wanting to eat but being unable to choose food or start preparing it. It is a community term for executive dysfunction applied to eating, and it is often worse when hunger has already become urgent.

### Meltdown

An involuntary reaction to overwhelming stress or sensory input, in which a person loses control of their responses. It may involve crying, shouting or physical agitation. It is not a tantrum, because it is neither chosen nor aimed at getting something.

### Monotropism

A theory of autism proposing that autistic attention tends to concentrate deeply on a small number of interests at once, instead of spreading across many. It is used to explain both the depth of autistic focus and the difficulty of switching between tasks.

### Neurodiversity

The idea that variation in how brains work, including autism and ADHD, is a natural part of human diversity. A neurodivergent person is someone whose brain works differently from the typical pattern.

### Rejection sensitive dysphoria

Intense emotional pain in response to real or perceived rejection, criticism or failure. The term is widely used in ADHD communities to describe something many people with ADHD recognise immediately. It is not a formal diagnosis and does not appear in diagnostic manuals.

### Revenge bedtime procrastination

Staying up late, even when tired, to reclaim personal time that the day did not allow. It is common among people with ADHD and anyone whose days are full of other people's demands.

### Rumination

Repetitive, circular thinking about the same worry or event without reaching a conclusion. It feels like problem-solving but produces no decisions, and it is often worst at night when there is nothing else to occupy attention.

### Sensory overload

When the amount or intensity of sensory input, such as noise, light, touch or smell, exceeds what the brain can process. It can cause distress, irritability, shutdown or meltdown. It is very common in autism and also occurs in ADHD.

### Shutdown

A response to overwhelm in which a person withdraws and becomes less responsive, sometimes temporarily losing the ability to speak or move easily. Like a meltdown it is involuntary, but the reaction turns inward rather than outward.

### Special interest

An intense, long-lasting interest that an autistic person finds deeply absorbing. Many autistic adults describe their special interests as a source of joy and regulation rather than simply a hobby.

### Spoon theory

A metaphor in which daily energy is a limited number of spoons, and every task, including small ones, costs some. It began in the chronic illness community and is now widely used by disabled and neurodivergent people to explain why capacity runs out.

### Stimming

Repetitive movements or sounds, such as rocking, hand-flapping, tapping, humming or fidgeting, used to self-regulate. It is common in autism and also occurs in ADHD. Many autistic adults were trained to suppress it as children.

### Task paralysis

Being unable to start a task despite wanting or needing to, sometimes to the point where beginning feels physically impossible. It is linked to executive dysfunction and is one of the most commonly described experiences of adult ADHD.

### Time blindness

Difficulty sensing the passage of time and estimating how long things will take, commonly reported by people with ADHD. It leads to lateness, missed deadlines and tasks that take far longer than expected. It is a community term rather than a clinical one.

### Unmasking

Gradually reducing masking, usually starting in private and extending selectively to safe people and places. It tends to be slow and partial, and safety has to come first.
